Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary on Surah 55, verses 1–4:

These words indicate that He, glorified is He, gives all the levels of existence in their entirety. His saying ﴿He created man﴾ is a report about the external, concrete bringing-into-being.

Man is singled out for creation because of what has preceded.

His saying ﴿He taught the Qur'an﴾ is a report about the granting of existence in knowledge and the mind. Man learned the Qur'an only through His teaching, just as he became a human only through His creating. He is the One who created him and taught him.

Then He said ﴿He taught him clear expression (al-bayan)﴾.

Al-bayan encompasses three levels, each of which is called bayan:

The first: the mental bayan, by which one distinguishes between the things known.

The second: the verbal bayan, by which one expresses those known things and conveys them to others.

The third: the written, inscribed bayan, by which those words are drawn so that the one who looks can understand their meanings, just as the listener understands the meanings of words.

So this is bayan for the eye, and that is bayan for the ear.

The first is bayan for the heart. Very often, glorified is He, He combines these three, as in His saying ﴿Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart — all of these will be questioned about﴾.

He also censures those who do not benefit from them in acquiring guidance and beneficial knowledge, as in His saying ﴿Deaf, dumb, blind﴾ and His saying ﴿Allah has sealed their hearts and their hearing, and over their sight is a veil﴾.

(Section)

Contemplate the wisdom in the creation of leaves. In a single leaf, from among the veins extending through it and dispersed within it, you will see things that dazzle the observer. Some of them are thick, extending lengthwise and widthwise, and among them are fine ones that thread through those thick ones, woven in a delicate and wondrous weave. Were this something that humans could undertake to make with their own hands, they would not finish one leaf in a full year, and they would need for it tools, movements, and treatments that their capacity would fail to achieve. Yet the All-Creating, the All-Knowing, scattered in a few days of that which fills the earth, its plains and its mountains, without tools, without helper, and without treatment. It is nothing but His penetrating will in everything and His power which nothing can resist. His command, when He wills a thing, is only to say to it, "Be," and it is.

Contemplate the wisdom in those veins threading through the whole leaf, so that they may water it and convey nourishment to it, preserving its life and freshness, in the same way as the veins dispersed in bodies that carry nourishment to every part of them. Contemplate also what the thick veins do in holding the leaf with their firmness and solidity, lest it tear and perish. They are like the nerves of an animal's body. You see that they have perfected their formation and extended the veins in their length and breadth so that they hold firm and the leaf does not suffer tearing. Then contemplate the wisdom of the Subtle, the All-Aware, in making them an adornment for the tree, a covering, a garment for the fruit, and a protection for it from the afflictions that prevent its perfection.

For this reason, when the tree is stripped of its leaves, the fruit spoils and is not benefited from. And look how the leaves were made a shield for the place of growth of the weak fruit against drying out. When the fruit is gone, the leaves remain as a shield for those weak branches against the heat, until that ember is extinguished, and the leaves do not harm the branches. Their hold is removed from them, and they are stripped of them so that they may be clothed in a new garment better than it. Blessed is God, Lord of the worlds, who knows the places where those leaves fall and their origins; no leaf falls out except by His permission, and it does not drop except by His knowledge.

Yet even so, if the servants were to witness them, in their multitude and variety, while they glorify their Lord along with the fruits, the branches and the trees, they would witness another aspect of their beauty, and would see their creation with another eye, and would know that they were created for a great matter, and that they were not created in vain. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And the star and the tree prostrate themselves﴾

So "the star" is what has no stem among plants, and "the tree" is what has a stem, and all of them prostrate themselves to God, glorifying Him with His praise: ﴿And there is not a thing but that it glorifies Him with His praise, but you do not understand their glorification. Indeed, He is Forbearing and Forgiving﴾

Perhaps you are one of those whose veil is thick, who holds that their glorification is only an indication of their Maker. Know that this view's falsehood becomes apparent from more than thirty aspects, most of which we have mentioned in another place.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 55, verse 12:**

(Section)

In *Sahih Muslim*, from the Prophet (ﷺ):

"Whoever is offered a *rayhan* (sweet basil, a fragrant plant), let him not refuse it, for it is light to carry and pleasant in scent."

In *Sunan Ibn Majah*, from the hadith of Usama (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Prophet (ﷺ) said:

"Is there anyone who strives for Paradise? For Paradise has no price. By the Lord of the Ka'bah, it is a light that shines, a *rayhanah* that sways, a lofty palace, a flowing river, ripe fruit, a beautiful and graceful wife, and many garments, in an abiding place, in silk and radiance, in lofty, sound and beautiful houses." They said, "Yes, O Messenger of Allah, we are those who strive for it." He said, "Say: *In sha' Allah* (if Allah wills)." So the people said, "In sha' Allah."

*Al-rayhan* (a term for fragrant plants) is every plant with a pleasant smell, and each people in each land attribute it to a particular plant. The people of the West attribute it to *al-ās* (myrtle), which is the one the Arabs know as *rayhan*, while the people of Iraq and Syria attribute it to *al-habaq* (a type of basil).

As for myrtle, its temperament is cold in the first degree and dry in the second. It is also composed of opposing qualities. Its predominant element is a cold earthy substance, and within it there is a subtle hot element. It dries strongly, and its parts are of similar strength. Its power is astringent, restraining from both within and without at once.

It stops bilious diarrhoea, repels hot moist vapour when smelled, and gladdens the heart greatly. Smelling it prevents plague, and so does spreading it in the house.

It cures swellings that arise in the two glands (of the neck or groin) when applied to them. When its fresh leaves are pounded and mixed with vinegar and placed on the head, they stop nosebleeds. When its dry leaves are ground and sprinkled on moist ulcers, they benefit them. It strengthens weak limbs when applied as a poultice, it benefits *dā' al-dāhis* (a skin condition), and when sprinkled on pustules and ulcers on the hands and feet, it benefits them.

When the body is rubbed with it, it stops sweating, dries excess moisture, and removes armpit odour. When one sits in its decoction, it benefits prolapse of the anus and womb, and loosening of the joints. When poured on fractures of bones that have not knitted, it benefits them.

It clears scalp scales, its moist sores and pustules. It holds back falling hair and darkens it. When its leaves are pounded, a little water is poured on them, mixed with some oil or rose oil, and applied as a poultice, it suits moist ulcers, *al-namlah* (a skin eruption), *al-humrah* (erysipelas), sharp swellings, *al-shara* (urticaria) and haemorrhoids.

Its seed benefits spitting of blood arising in the chest and lungs. It astringes the stomach. It is not harmful to the chest or lungs, because of its mildness. Its special property is benefit in looseness of the bowels accompanied by coughing, which is rare among medicines. It promotes urine, benefits irritation of the bladder, the bite of the tarantula, and the sting of scorpions. Rubbing oneself with its juice, however, is harmful, so one should beware of this.

As for the Persian basil, which is called *al-habaq*, it is hot according to one of the two opinions. Smelling it benefits hot headaches when water is sprinkled on it. It cools, and moistens incidentally. According to the other opinion it is cold. Is it moist or dry? There are two opinions on this.

The correct view is that it contains the four temperaments. It induces sleep. Its seed stops bilious diarrhoea, calms colic, strengthens the heart, and benefits melancholic diseases.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on Surah 55, verses 17–18:**

(Section: The East and the West, between Plural, Dual and Singular Forms)

Among this same meaning is the occurrence of "al-mashriq" (the east) and "al-maghrib" (the west) in the Qur'an, sometimes in the plural, sometimes in the dual, and sometimes in the singular, because each context is specific to what it requires of that form. The first is like His saying: ﴿So I swear by the Lord of the easts and the wests﴾.

The second is like His saying: ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests. So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?﴾

The third is like His saying: ﴿Lord of the East and the West; there is no god but He, so take Him as a Guardian﴾.

So reflect on this profound wisdom in the variation of these passages in singular, plural and dual forms according to their contexts; it will reveal to you the greatness and majesty of the Noble Qur'an, and that it is a revelation from the All-Wise, the Praiseworthy. Wherever the plural is used, the intended meaning is the risings and settings of the sun throughout the days of the year, which are many. Wherever the singular is used, the intended meaning is the two horizons of east and west. Wherever the dual is used, the intended meaning is the two easts of its ascent and descent and their two wests, for it begins by ascending until it reaches the furthest point of its height and elevation. This is the east of its ascent, and from it arise the autumn and winter seasons. So he made the east of its ascent, in its entirety, one east, and the east of its descent, in its entirety, one east, and their two wests correspond to them. This is the reason for the difference of these in singular, dual and plural forms.

As for the reason each passage is specific to what occurs in it, I have not seen anyone address it or open its door, and it is, praise be to God, clear from the context.

Reflect on its occurrence in the dual in Surah al-Rahman, since the course of the surah is the course of pairs and couplings. It first mentions the two kinds of origination, namely creation and exaltation; then it mentions the two lamps of the world and the two manifesters of its light, namely the sun and the moon; then it mentions the two kinds of plants, that which stands upon a stalk and that which spreads upon the face of the earth, namely the star and the tree; then it mentions the two kinds of the raised heaven and the laid-down earth, and informs that He raised this and laid down this, and placed between them the mention of the balance, then the mention of justice and injustice in the balance, so He commanded justice and forbade injustice; it mentions the two kinds that come out of the earth, namely grains and fruits; then it mentions the creation of the two kinds of the accountable, namely the human kind and the jinn kind; then it mentions the two easts and the two wests;

then after that it mentions the two seas, the salty and the sweet. So reflect on the fitness of the dual form of east and west in this surah and the grandeur of their occurrence for this reason, and estimate their place with the word in singular or plural, and you will find the hearing recoiling from it and the intellect bearing witness to its incompatibility with the arrangement.

Then reflect on their occurrence in the singular in Surah al-Muzzammil, since the mention of night and day preceded them. He commanded His Messenger ﷺ to stand in prayer at night, then informed him that he has in the day a long occupation. When the mention of the night and what he was commanded in it preceded, and the mention of the day and what occurs in it, the mention of the east and the west followed, which are the manifestation of night and day. Their occurrence in the singular in this context was better than the dual or plural, because the appearance of night and day is one; the day always appears from the east, and the night always appears from the west.

Then reflect on their occurrence in the plural in Surah al-Ma'arij in His saying: ﴿So I swear by the Lord of the easts and the wests, indeed We are able to replace them with better than them, and We are not to be outdone﴾.

Since this oath is in the context of the breadth of His lordship and the comprehensiveness of His power, and what is sworn to is the lords of those people and bringing better than them, He mentioned the easts and the wests, because they include the movement of the sun, which is one of His great and mighty signs, and His transporting it and turning it each day through an east and a west. Whoever does this, how could He be incapable of replacing those and bringing to their places something better than them? Moreover, the effect of the easts and wests of the sun on the variation of the states of plants and animals is well known, and God, in His wisdom, has made that a cause for the change of the bodies of plants and the states of animals and their transition from one state to another; He alters heat by cold and cold by heat, summer by winter and winter by summer, and the rest of the changes of the states of animals and plants, winds, rains, snows and other transformations and alterations occurring in the world, due to the variation of the easts and wests of the sun. That is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing. So how could He not be able, in view of what they witness of that, to replace them with better? He emphasised this meaning with His saying ﴿and We are not to be outdone﴾, so nothing fits this place but the plural form.

Then reflect on how it also came in the plural in Surah as-Saffat in His saying: ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and Lord of the easts﴾.

Since it came together with the multiple objects of lordship, namely the heavens and the earth and what is between them, it was better that it came in the plural, to align with what precedes of plurality and multiplicity. Then reflect on how He restricted it to the easts without the wests, because the situation required that. The easts are the manifestation of lights and the means of the spreading, life, movement, livelihood and expansion of animals; this is a visible creation, so He placed it before the refutation of those who deny resurrection. Then He mentioned the wonder of His servants at their denial and their deeming resurrection after death unlikely, then the measure of death and their state in it. Restricting the mention to the easts here was most fitting to the intended purpose, and God knows best...

(Section)

Ibn al-Qayyim said in (al-Tibyan fi Aqsam al-Qur'an):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾.

It has been said: they are the east of summer and the east of winter. Each place has what fits it: in Surah al-Rahman came ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾,

because it is a surah in which pairs are mentioned. In it are mentioned creation and teaching, the sun and the moon, the stars and the trees, the heaven and the earth, the grain and the fruit, the jinn and mankind, the origin of the father of mankind and the father of the jinn, the two seas, the Garden and the Fire, and the division of the Garden into two high gardens and two lower than them.

It informs that in each garden there are two springs. So it fits perfectly that the two easts and the two wests be mentioned.

(Section)

Al-Tirmidhi mentioned from the hadith of Jabir ibn Abdullah, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said:

"The Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out to his companions and recited to them Surah al-Rahman from beginning to end. They were silent, so he said: 'I recited it to the jinn on the night of the jinn, and they were better in response than you. Every time I came to His saying ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ they said: "None of Your blessings, our Lord, do we deny. To You be praise."'"

The phrase "in it" was not used because, at the time of annihilation, the state is not one of settled abode and establishment.

[Section: Annihilation (al-Fana')]
The author of al-Manazil said: (Chapter on Annihilation). God Most High said: ﴿Everyone upon it is passing away﴾ [al-Rahman: 26]. ﴿And there remains the Face of your Lord, Lord of Majesty and Honour﴾ [al-Rahman: 27].

The annihilation mentioned in the verse is not the annihilation to which the Sufi group (al-ta'ifah) refers. Rather, the annihilation in the verse is ruin and non-existence. He, glorified is He, informed that everyone on the earth will be destroyed and will die, and His Face remains. This is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, you will die, and indeed they will die﴾ [al-Zumar: 30],
and like His saying: ﴿Every soul will taste death﴾ [Al 'Imran: 185].

Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: When this verse was revealed, the angels said: "The people of the earth have perished." Then when He, Most High, said: ﴿Everything will perish except His Face﴾ [al-Qasas: 88], the angels were certain of the perishing.

Al-Sha'bi said: When you recite ﴿Everyone upon it is passing away﴾ [al-Rahman: 26], do not stop until you recite ﴿And there remains the Face of your Lord, Lord of Majesty﴾ [al-Rahman: 27].

This is from his understanding of the Qur'an and the completeness of his knowledge, since the intended meaning is the report of the passing away of those upon it together with the remaining of the Face of God, glorified is He. The verse was brought to praise Him with sole permanence, and the mere passing away of creation does not in itself contain His praise; the praise lies in His remaining after the passing away of His creation. Thus it is a parallel to His saying: ﴿Everything will perish except His Face﴾ [al-Qasas: 88].

As for the annihilation that the Sufi group expresses, it is a matter other than this. But the verse indicates that the annihilation referred to is the departure of the heart, its leaving this world and its attachment to the Exalted, the Great, to whom belongs permanence, so that annihilation does not reach Him. Whoever is annihilated in His love, obedience, and seeking of His Face, this annihilation brings him to the station of permanence. So the verse indicates that the servant ought not to attach himself to one who is passing away, and abandon the One who has permanence, Lord of Majesty and Honour. It is as if it says: if you attach yourself to one who is passing away, that attachment is cut off at his passing away precisely when you are most in need of him; but if you attach yourself to one who is permanent and does not pass away, your attachment is not cut off and endures by His enduring.

The annihilation to which the Sufis refer is the ultimate and final point of attachment, for it is cutting off from everything other than the Lord, Most High, in every respect. Therefore he said:
"Annihilation in this chapter is the dissolving of what is beneath the Truth: first in knowledge, then in denial, then in reality."

I say: "Annihilation" is the opposite of "permanence," and the permanent is either permanent in itself, without need of anyone to preserve it, its permanence being one of the necessities of its own essence, and this is God alone; or everything else, whose permanence is by the permanence of the Lord, and which has no permanence of its own essence, just as it has no existence of its own essence. Its bringing into being and its preservation come from its Lord and Creator; otherwise it has of itself nothing but non-existence before its bringing into being, and annihilation after its bringing into being.

The meaning is not that its essence and self require its non-existence and annihilation. Rather, annihilation means that if you consider its essence, setting aside the bringing into being by its Originator, it would be non-existent; and if you consider it after its existence, setting aside its preservation by its Originator, its permanence would be impossible, for it persists only by His preservation, just as it is brought into existence only by His bringing into being. This is the meaning of our saying that it is, in itself, non-existent and passing away. So understand this.

People have differed: does the annihilation and destruction of what exists occur by the creation of an accident in it, which is called annihilation and destruction, or by withholding the creation of permanence for it, since at every moment it needs Him to create for it a permanence that sustains it? This is the well-known question of destruction (al-i'dam).

The verification in it is that its essence does not require existence; it is non-existent in itself. So when the Lord, Most High, decrees for its existence a term and a time, its existence ends when its term arrives, and it returns to its origin, which is non-existence. Yes, He may decree for it a time and then erase that time, intending its destruction before its time, just as He, glorified is He, erases what He wills and affirms what He wills, and He may intend the continuation of its existence beyond the decreed time until another appointed term. He erases what He wills and affirms. God Most High said, quoting His Prophet Nuh, peace be upon him: ﴿He said: "O my people, I am to you a clear warner, that you worship God and fear Him and obey me; He will forgive you some of your sins and delay you until a specified term"﴾ [Nuh: 2-4]. So when God, glorified is He, wills the preservation of a thing, He preserves it until the time He wills; and when He wills its annihilation, He causes it to be non-existent by His will, just as He brings it into being by His will.

If it is said: the object of will must necessarily be an existential matter, so how can non-existence be the object of will?

It is said: the object of will is two things: bringing into being and destruction, and both are possible. So the claim that the object of will must necessarily be an existential matter is a false assertion. Yes, pure non-existence is not the object of will; but destruction (al-i'dam) is more specific than non-existence.

Had we not been concerned with a more specific matter than this, we would have expanded the discussion on this question and mentioned the delusions and errors of people concerning it.

As for his saying: "Annihilation is the name for the dissolving of what is beneath the Truth in knowledge," he means: it dissolves from the heart and from witnessing in knowledge, even if its essence is not in the present state annihilated and dissolved. Thus the forms of existents disappear from the witnessing of the servant, such that they are as if they had entered non-existence, as they were before they came into being, and the Truth, Most High, Lord of Majesty and Honour, remains alone in the heart of the witness, as He was alone before the creation of the worlds.

His saying: "in knowledge, then in denial, then in reality": these three are the stages of dissolving when it comes upon the servant in sequence. If it comes all at once, he does not witness any of that, though he may recognize it when he returns to his knowledge and witnessing. When the Lord, glorified is He, elevates His servant gradually, He illuminates his inner self and intellect with knowledge, so he sees that there is no creator besides Him, no lord other than Him, that none besides Him possesses harm, benefit, giving, or withholding, and that none besides Him deserves to be worshipped with utmost submission and love; and every object of worship other than His noble Face is false. This is the tawhid of knowledge.

Then when the Truth, glorified is He, elevates him a degree above this, He makes him witness the return of the created things to His acts, glorified is He, and the return of His acts to His names and attributes, and the subsistence of His attributes in His essence. Thus the witnessing of other than Him dissolves from his heart, and he denies that anything whatsoever of himself belongs to other than Him. A sound person does not deny as the heretics deny, for that denial is itself heresy.

Then when He elevates him another degree, He makes him witness the subsistence of all the worlds, their substances and accidents, their essences and attributes, by Him alone, that is, by His establishing them and His holding them. For He, glorified is He, holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease, holds the seas lest they overflow or spill over the world, holds the sky lest it fall upon the earth, holds the birds in flight, spreading their wings and folding them, holds the hearts of the certain lest they swerve from faith, holds the life of animals lest it leave them before the appointed term, and holds the existence of existents upon them; were it not for that, they would dissolve and vanish. All stands by His acts and attributes, which are among the necessities of His essence. So true existence belongs to Him alone, meaning the existence which is independent of everything other than Him, while everything other than Him is poor in need of Him by essence, having no standing in itself for the blink of an eye.

And since annihilation has a beginning, a middle, and an end, he indicated its three stages: the first stage is the annihilation of the people of knowledge who are realized in it; the second is the annihilation of the people of conduct and will; and the third is the annihilation of the people of gnosis, who are absorbed in witnessing the Truth, glorified is He.

At the outset, the strength of his knowledge and his awareness of created beings perishes in comparison with his knowledge and recognition of God and His rights. Then this grows until he counts them as the dead and as non-existent. Then this grows until he is absent from them, such that he is addressed and does not hear, and passes by them and does not see; and this is more profound than the state of intoxication. But this state does not last for him, and he cannot remain living in it.

[Stages of Annihilation]
[Section: The First Degree, Annihilation of Knowledge in the Known]
He said: It has three degrees. The first degree: the annihilation of the knower in the known, which is annihilation in knowledge; the annihilation of sight in the seen, which is annihilation in denial; and the annihilation of seeking in existence, which is annihilation in reality.

This is a detailed explanation of what he stated in summary at first, and we will clarify what they meant by knowledge, denial, and reality.

As for the annihilation of knowing in the known: it is the absence of the knower from awareness of his knowing and its meanings, so he is annihilated in Him, glorified is He, from his own attribute here and what subsists in him. For knowing is His act and attribute; when he is absorbed in witnessing the known, he is annihilated from the attribute of his own self and its act. Since knowing is above knowledge and more specific than it, the annihilation of knowing in the known entails the annihilation of knowledge in knowing; so he is annihilated first in knowing, then knowing is annihilated in the known.

As for the annihilation of sight in the seen: sight is above knowing, for knowing is a station above knowledge and below sight. When he moves from knowing to sight, his sight is annihilated in what he sees, just as his knowing was annihilated in what he knows.

As for the annihilation of seeking in existence: it is that no seeking remains for the possessor of this annihilation, because he has attained the sought, which is witnessed, and has become a finder after having been a seeker. His perception was first knowledge, then it strengthened and became knowing, then it strengthened and became sight, then it was firmly established and became knowing, then it was firmly established and became existence.

Perhaps you find these terms and their meanings strange or far-fetched, so listen to an illustrative example that will ease this for you and bring it near: like a king of great authority, of severe might, of complete awe, of strong power, who summoned a man from his subjects whose offence and rebellion against him had grown grave. He came before him, and it was assumed that he would be destroyed. His states during his presence vary according to what he witnesses. At times he remembers his offence and the king's might and his power over him, so he thinks of what he will meet; at times the state he is in overwhelms him, so he does not recall what he has done nor why he was summoned, because fear dominates his heart and he despairs of deliverance; yet his intellect and mind remain with him. At times his heart and mind are completely absent, so he does not perceive where he is, nor who is beside him, nor what is intended for him; and perhaps in this state there escapes from his tongue what he does not intend. This is the annihilation of fear.

A second example, of the annihilation of love: a lover whose love has absorbed him in a person of utmost beauty and splendour, whose greatest wish is to reach him, converse with him, and see him. While he is in his state, his heart filled with love and his thought absorbed in his beloved, suddenly his beloved enters upon him unexpectedly in the most beautiful form, and he meets him close by, with nothing between them. Is it not fitting that he be annihilated from witnessing himself by the one witnessed, indeed from his love for himself by his beloved? So the beloved takes possession of his hearing, sight, will, and sensation, and he is absent from his essence and attributes by him? Look at the women, how they cut their hands when Joseph appeared to them and they beheld that beauty, though they had not previously experienced such passion and love as the wife of the Aziz had; the witnessing of his beauty annihilated them from their own state, until they cut their hands.

As for the wife of the Aziz: though she was the one with love, she had grown accustomed to seeing and beholding him, so when he went out her state did not change upon her as it changed upon the blamers. Thus her station was permanence and theirs was annihilation, and annihilation came to them in two respects.

The first: their heedlessness of awareness of cutting what was in their hands, until the cutting passed beyond to the hands.

The second: their annihilation from sensing the pain of the cutting. Thus annihilation through what is feared, and joy through what is loved, annihilates its possessor from his awareness and from his sensing of the psychic conditions.

This is the commentary on the verse. It concerns the sight of a created, originated being, which has likenesses and equals, and has others who approach it and rival it in beauty. Its superiority over its own kind in beauty and comeliness is only in some attributes, and it is distinguished only by some created, fashioned qualities. So what is the assumption about the One to whom all beauty belongs, all perfection, all goodness and all completeness? The proportion of every beauty in existence to His beauty and majesty is less than the proportion of a feeble lamp to the very sun. When He, glorified is He, knew that the faculties of human beings cannot bear, in this abode, the seeing of Him, He veiled Himself from His servants until the Day of Resurrection, and He will bring them into a creation by which they will be able to witness His beauty and see His Face. And you see some of His signs, His creatures and His originated things, how the one who witnesses them is annihilated in them from everything else. But all of this concerns the sensory witnessings and the emotional experiences.

As for the divine knowledges, the state of "subsistence" (al-baqa') in them is more complete than the state of "annihilation" (al-fana'), and this is the state of our Prophet, the prayers and peace of Allah be upon him, and the state of the perfected among his followers. For this reason he saw what he saw on the night of the Isra' and the Mi'raj while his heart was steady, his composure firm, his perception present, and his discernment complete; and if another had seen some of that, he would not have been able to contain himself.

If you say: perhaps I understand the meaning of the annihilation of knowledge in the known and the annihilation of sight in the seen, but what is the meaning of the annihilation of seeking in existence, such that it is truly the annihilation? I say: when you understand the two matters that precede it, you understand its meaning. For the seeker, when he has attained his existent object, his seeking for it ceases and dissolves, and this is observed in the witnessed world. You see the seeker of an important matter: when his hands have grasped it and he has attained it, how does his seeking cool and become annihilated in its existence? But this is impossible with regard to the knower, for his seeking does not leave him; rather, when he finds, his seeking intensifies, so he is always seeking. Whenever he has more finding, he has more seeking. Yes, what is annihilated is the seeking of his own portion in seeking his Beloved and seeking His pleasure, and there is no end beyond this. But what the people (al-qawm, the Sufis) point to is this: that the servant, in the station of love, knowledge and immersion in witnessing, reaches a state in which the various kinds of nearness and the effects of the attributes take control over him, to the extent that his intellect is stunned away from his awareness of his seeking, his will and his love.

The clarification of this: when the servant turns toward his Lord, examines his own states, and becomes able to witness his Lord's standing over him, he is at first striving, patient and steadfast on guard. When he is patient, perseveres and remains on guard—patient within himself, persevering against his enemy, and standing guard at the frontier of his heart lest any thought enter it which his Master does not love—there then appears in his heart a light from his turning toward his Lord. When that light grows strong, it veils him from his mental existence and carries him through the hidden folds of the Unseen. Then his turning toward his Lord becomes pure for him, and when that is pure for him he is absent from his concrete and mental existence, absent by the light of his turning toward his Lord, through the arrival of pure remembrance and its clarity into his heart, where it is emptied of every preoccupation of concrete and mental existence, and he becomes one for the One. The light of watchfulness then takes control over the parts of his inner being, his heart fills with the light of devotion to the point that it floods his heart and covers it from everything else. Then that light flows from his inner being and pervades the parts of his outer being, so that the outer and the inner become alike in him. At that point the servant is annihilated from everything other than Him, and he subsists with the spiritual, essential witnessing which necessitates the special love that ignites the spirit.

Among them is one who weakens because of the scantiness of what comes to him, so he cannot make room for anything other than what the effects of special love have touched in his secret and heart. And among them is one who grows strong and whose vision widens, so he finds the traces of majesty and sacred beauty in his heart and spirit, and he finds worship and love, supplication and dependence, trust, fear and hope, and all the other acts of the heart standing within his heart, not preoccupying him from the witnessing of the spirit, nor does the absorbed witnessing of the spirit make him oblivious to them. He finds his attentiveness to the commands and prohibitions present at the root of his heart, where the trust was deposited, so the absorbing witnessing of the spirit does not preoccupy him, nor does the witnessing of the heart prevent him from observing the pleasure of the Lord, may He be exalted, His loves and His right over His servant. He finds the abandoning of planning and choosing, and the soundness of entrusting, existing in the seat of his self, so he deals with Allah, glorified is He, by that, such that the witnessing of the First does not preoccupy him from Him. He observes with his intellect the secrets of the wisdom of Allah in His creation and His command, and all of that does not veil him from observing his servanthood. Thus he remains with his spirit immersed in observing the singularity, its majesty, its perfection and its beauty, his love and longing for Him having overwhelmed him, his heart filled with the worship of the hearts, his heart filled with observing wisdom and the meanings of the address, his heart pure of base morals, both with Allah, the Exalted, and with creation. He has become a pure servant of his Lord with his spirit, heart, intellect, self, body and limbs. Each has fulfilled what is due of servanthood, such that the servanthood of one part does not veil him from the servanthood of another part. He has annihilated from his self and subsists by his Lord, as Abu Bakr al-Kattani said: A question about love arose in Mecca during the season, and the shaykhs spoke about it. al-Junayd was the youngest of them in age, so they said to him: "Speak what you have, O Iraqi!" He lowered his gaze for a while, his eyes shed tears, then he said: "A servant who has departed from his self, connected to the remembrance of his Lord, standing in discharging His rights, looking at Him with his heart, whose heart the lights of His awe have burned, whose drink from the cup of His affection has been made pure, and to whom the Almighty has been revealed from the veils of His unseen. If he speaks, it is by Allah; if he utters, it is from Allah; if he acts, it is by the command of Allah; if he is still, it is with Allah. He is for Allah, by Allah, and with Allah."

The shaykhs wept and said: "There is nothing beyond this. May Allah reward you, O crown of the knowers."

[Section: The Second Degree: the annihilation of the witnessing of seeking, by its removal]

The Shaykh said: The second degree: the annihilation of the witnessing of seeking through its removal, the annihilation of the witnessing of knowledge through its removal, and the annihilation of the witnessing of direct vision through its removal.

This degree of annihilation is higher in his view than what precedes it, because it is more complete in annihilation from the perspective of its practitioners' annihilation from their own annihilation. The mention of their states and stations has fallen from their hearts because of their preoccupation with their Lord.

His phrase "through its removal" means the removal of the witnessing, not the removal of the witnessed. The seeking, the knowledge and the direct vision remain, but the witnessing has fallen away, because its possessor is absorbed in the witnessed object of vision.

[Section: The Third Degree: the annihilation from the witnessing of annihilation]

He said: The third degree: annihilation from the witnessing of annihilation, which is annihilation in truth, glancing at the lightning of the eye, riding the sea of unification, traveling the path of subsistence.

The difference between annihilation in this degree and the one before it is that in the earlier one he has passed away from witnessing his seeking, knowledge and sight, while being conscious of his passing away from them; whereas in this degree he has passed away from all of that and passed away from witnessing his own annihilation, as it is said: "The last to die is the Angel of Death."

This annihilation is, in his view, annihilation in truth, because in it everything other than the Real, glorified is He, has been annihilated, for its possessor witnesses that annihilation has occurred, so nothing remains except the One, the Subduer.

His phrase "glancing at the lightning of the eye": the one who glances (al-sha'im) is the one who looks from afar, and "the lightning of the eye" is the light of reality. It has already been noted that this cannot refer to external light; rather, it is the lights of nearness, watchfulness and presence with Allah.

His phrase "riding the sea of unification": the "unification" (al-jam') to which they point is an expression for the gaze of insight rising toward the mere source of all scattered things, as will be explained in its own chapter, God willing. Riding the depths of this unification is annihilation within it.

His phrase "traveling the path of subsistence" means: whoever has passed away has become qualified for subsistence through the Real. This subsistence comes after annihilation, for when one is established in annihilation, the banner of reality is raised for him, so he hastens toward it traveling the path of subsistence, which is standing by the litanies and guarding the states that come. At that point, arrival is hoped for him.

(Section)

Neither the Book nor the Sunnah, nor the words of the Companions and the Successors, praise or blame the term "annihilation" (fana'); they never used this term in the sense referred to here, nor did the earlier masters of the path mention it or make it an ultimate goal or a station. The people (the early generations) were more worthy of every perfection and more ahead to every praiseworthy goal. We do not reject this term absolutely, nor do we accept it absolutely.

It requires detail, and the sound must be distinguished from the flawed, its means from its end. So we say, and with Allah is success, and He is the Opener, the All-Knowing:

The reality of the "annihilation" referred to is the dissolution of a thing in mental, cognitive existence. Here the people of uprightness and the people of deviation and atheism have divided it. The people of union (ittihad), who hold the doctrine of the unity of existence, claim that annihilation is the ultimate annihilation from the existence of anything else, so that no existence at all remains for anything other, neither in witnessing nor in direct vision. Rather, one realizes through witnessing the unity of existence, and then knows that the existence of all existents is the very existence of the Real; there are not two existences, but only one existent. For them the reality of annihilation is to pass away from what has no reality, rather is illusion and imagination, passing away from what is itself perishing and has no existence, and so one witnesses the annihilation of the existence of everything else in His existence. This is pure expression; otherwise, in reality, for these people there is no "other" nor "different," and the other and the different exist only in illusion and imagination. Around this annihilation they hover and circle.

As for the people of tawhid and uprightness, they refer by annihilation to two matters, one of which is higher than the other.

The first matter: annihilation in the witnessing of lordship and self-subsistence. One witnesses the Lord, exalted is He, as alone in self-subsistence and governance, in creating and providing, in giving and withholding, in harm and benefit, and that all existents are acted upon, not agents, and whatever act they have is an acted-upon act, a pure locus for the rulings of lordship to flow through it, possessing none of these for itself or for another, not owning harm or benefit. When the servant is established in this witnessing, thoughts and volitions in him grow still, looking toward the Self-Subsisting in whose hand is the governance of affairs, and moving toward His will and wisdom; he looks from Him, by Him, toward Him, passing away by witnessing Him from witnessing anything else. Yet with this he strives to attain Him, standing in obligatory and voluntary acts.

The second matter: annihilation in the witnessing of divinity. Its reality is annihilation from willing anything other than Allah, and from loving it, and from turning in repentance to anything else, and from relying on anything else, and from fearing and hoping in anything else. So one passes away in his love for Him from loving anything else, and in his fear and hope of Him from fearing or hoping in anything else. The reality of this annihilation is singling out the Lord, glorified is He, with love, fear and hope, reverence and veneration. We will indicate the beginnings of this, its middle and its end, so we say:

Know that when the heart is free of preoccupation with this world and of attachment to what it holds, whether wealth, rank or appearance, and attaches itself to the Hereafter, concerning itself with gathering provision for it and preparing to meet God, Mighty and Majestic, then this is the first of its openings and the first light of its dawn. At that point the heart begins to move toward knowing what its Lord is pleased with from it, so that it does that and draws near to Him through it, and toward knowing what displeases Him, so that it avoids that. This is the sign of the sincerity of its intention. Whoever is certain of meeting God, and that He will question him about two words, about which the first and the last will be questioned, "What were you worshipping? And how did you answer the Messengers?", must awaken to seeking knowledge of the One he worships and the path that leads to Him. When he becomes firmly established in this, God opens for him the door of intimacy through solitude, seclusion and empty places where voices and movements are still. Nothing is more longed for by him than this, for it gathers upon him the powers of his heart and his will, and it closes off the doors that scatter his concern and disperse his heart. So he finds intimacy in them and feels estranged from creation.

Then He opens for him the door of the sweetness of worship, so that he can hardly get enough of it, and he finds in it pleasure and ease many times greater than what he used to find in the pleasure of amusement, play and the attainment of desires. To the extent that when he enters prayer, he wishes never to leave it. Then He opens for him the door of the sweetness of hearing the speech of God, so that he is never satisfied with it. When he hears it, his heart is calmed by it, as a child is calmed when given something it loves most. Then He opens for him the door of witnessing the greatness of God, the One who speaks it, His majesty, the perfection of His attributes, qualities and wisdom, and the meanings of His address, to the extent that his heart becomes absorbed in this until he vanishes within it. He senses in his heart that he has entered another world, different from the one in which people are.

Then He opens for him the door of shame before God, which is the first of the witnesses of knowledge. It is a light that falls into the heart; that light shows him that he is standing before his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, so he feels shame before Him in his privacy and in his public life. At that point he is granted constant vigilance over the Watcher and constant longing for the presence of the Most High, until it is as though he sees Him and witnesses Him above His heavens, established upon His Throne, looking at His creation, hearing their voices, and observing their inner selves. When this witness takes hold of him, it veils from him many of the worldly concerns and what they contain. He is in one state of being while people are in another. He is in a state of being before his Lord and his Protector, looking at Him with his heart, while people are behind the veil of the world of visible witness. He sees them, but they do not see him, and they do not see from him except what suits their world and their existence.

Then He opens for him the door of awareness of the witnessing of self-subsistence (al-qayyūmiyya), so he sees all the cosmic transformations and the turnings of existence in the hand of Him alone, glorified is He. He witnesses Him as the Owner of harm and benefit, of creation and provision, of giving life and causing death. So he takes Him alone as his Trustee, and he is content with Him as Lord, Manager and Sufficient. At that point, whenever his gaze falls upon any of the created things, it guides him to its Creator and Originator, and to the attributes of His perfection and the qualities of His majesty. His creation does not veil Him from him, glorified is He. Rather, each of the created things calls out to him with the tongue of its state: "Listen to my testimony for the One who perfected everything He created; I am the handiwork of God, who perfected everything."

When this continues for him, He opens for him the door of contraction and expansion (al-qabḍ wa-l-basṭ). He contracts him until he feels the pain of contraction because of the strength of what has come upon him. Then He contracts his receptacle with the lights of existence, so that he passes away from his own existence and is effaced, as the light of the sun effaces the light of the stars. He folds the cosmos away from his heart, so that nothing remains in it but God, the One, the Subduer. The lights of knowledge, of practice, of truthfulness, of sincerity and of love overflow from his heart, as the light of the sun overflows from its body. Then he is immersed in the lights, as the rider of the sea is immersed in the sea. This happens only through discipline, striving, the removal of the rulings of human nature, and long standing at the door.

This is the knowledge of certainty (ʿilm al-yaqīn), not the eye of certainty (ʿayn al-yaqīn), nor the truth of certainty (ḥaqq al-yaqīn), since there is no way to reach those two in this abode. The eye of certainty is direct witnessing, and the truth of certainty is direct contact. Yes, the truth of certainty may occur in this world in relation to mental existence and what subsists in hearts alone, and nothing more, as has been established many times before. We are not deterred in this matter by the blame of any blamer. As for them, they are not deterred, regarding the fact that this is in direct vision, by any blame, and they are, in our view, truthful but deceived. We, in their view, are veiled from this and have not reached it.

If he continues in his state, standing at the door of his Master, not turning aside to the right or to the left, and not responding to anyone except the one calling him to Him, and knowing that the matter lies beyond this and that he has not yet arrived, then whenever he imagines that he has arrived, the increase is cut off from him. He is hoped to be granted another opening, above what he was in, his heart absorbed in the lights of witnessing majesty after the appearance of the lights of the True Existence and the effacing of his own existence. He should not imagine that the existence of His attributes and His essence will perish. Rather, what perishes is his soulful, natural existence, and there remains for him a spiritual, angelic, heart-based existence. So his heart remains swimming in a sea of lights from the traces of majesty, and the lights gush from within him as water gushes from a spring, until he finds the highest dominion as though it were within his inner self and his heart. He finds his heart elevated above all of that, ascending to the One above whom there is nothing. Then God, glorified is He, raises him further and shows him the lights of generosity after he has witnessed the lights of majesty. He is immersed in a light from the rays of beauty. In this witnessing he tastes the special love that inflames spirits and hearts, and the heart remains captivated in the hand of its Beloved and its Protector, tested by His love. If you wish to understand this approximately, look at yourself and at others, when you have been tested by a form of wondrous beauty, outwardly and inwardly. It takes possession of your heart, your thought, your night and your day, and a fire of love is kindled for you, burning in your entrails, so that patience becomes difficult. That is the grace of God, which He gives to whom He wills.

How wondrous is a tested heart, immersed and absorbed in what has appeared to it of the rays of the lights of the One beauty, while people are tempted and tested by what passes away of wealth, forms and rank, tormented by that before obtaining it, during its obtaining, and after obtaining it. The highest of them in rank is one who is tempted by the dark-eyed maidens (ḥūr ʿīn), or who busies himself with enjoying the food, drink, clothing and marriage in Paradise. But this lover has risen through the degrees of love above the people of the stations. They look at him in Paradise as they look at a bright star that sets on the horizon, because of the height of his rank, the nearness of his station to his Beloved, and his companionship with Him. A person is with whom he loves, and for every deed there is a recompense. The recompense of love is love, arrival, closeness, and being chosen. This is what is fitting. Enough of that is honor and pride in this world's present life. So what do you think of their lofty stations with a Sovereign who is Omnipotent? How much more so when you see them on the Day of Resurrection, when the herald has made them hear: "Let every people go with what they used to worship." So they remain in their place, waiting for their God and their Beloved, who is the dearest thing to them, until He comes to them. They look at Him, and He manifests Himself to them, smiling.

The point is: God continues to elevate this servant layer after layer and station after station, until He brings him to Himself and establishes him before Him. Or he dies on the path, and his reward falls upon God. So the happy one is the one who is fully happy, and the one granted success is the one fully granted success: whoever does not turn aside from his Lord, blessed and exalted is He, to the right or to the left, and does not take anyone other than Him as Lord, Trustee, Beloved, Manager, Judge, Helper or Provider.

All of the stages of arrival mentioned above are only witnesses and examples. When the realities are revealed to him in the unseen, according to his readiness, his subtlety and his tenderness, from a place he does not see, a witness appears in his heart from their manifestation. That witness indicates them, but it is not them. For the light of majesty in the heart is not the light of the Possessor of Majesty outside. That would not be borne by the heavens and the earth, and if it appeared to existence, it would crush it to dust. Rather, it is a witness that points to that, just as the Most High Example is a witness pointing to the Essence. The Truth is beyond all of that, transcendent above incarnation, union, and mixing with His creation. These are only subtle perceptions and witnesses that stand in the heart of the knower, indicating the nearness of the subtle favors to him in the world of the unseen where he sees them. When he passes away, he passes away through his own state, not through God and not in Him. When he remains, he remains through his own state and his description, not through the subsistence of his Lord and His attributes. Nothing remains through God except God. Nevertheless, arrival is real. The one who arrives finds the traces of the manifestation of the attributes in his heart, and the traces of the manifestation of the Truth in his heart. He stations the heart above all the cosmos before the Lord, exalted is He, while He is upon His Throne. From there he is unveiled to the traces of majesty and generosity, and he finds the Throne and the Footstool beneath the witness of his heart in terms of rulings. What he finds beneath his heart is not, in reality, the Throne and the Footstool. It is a witness and a knowledge-based image, indicating the nearness of his heart to his Lord and the nearness of his Lord to his heart. There is a difference between the two tastes. When the Lord, exalted is He, draws near to the heart of His servant, the whole cosmos remains beneath the witness of his heart. Then the sun of tawḥīd rises on his horizon, by which the mist of his existence is dispelled, dissolves and vanishes. His self and his reality exist, separate from his Lord, and his Lord is separate from him. At that point the servant becomes absent from his self and passes away, yet in reality he remains, not perishing. But there is nothing in his innermost being except God. He has passed away in Him from everything other than Him.

Yes, it may happen to him in this state that he finds nothing other than God. That is because his heart is absorbed in what he witnesses and what exists for him. Had that been in the reality of the matter, the servant in this state would be a creator, an originator, a fashioner, eternal and everlasting.

So hold to this distinction, and beware of two groups who are the worst enemies of this affair: the group of the Jahmiyya, the Mu'aṭṭila, who have nothing above the Throne but pure nonexistence, so that even smelling the scent of this station from the farthest places is forbidden to them; and the group of the people of union (ahl al-ittiḥād), who say that the unity of existence (waḥdat al-wujūd) is true, and that the servant, in this journey, ends by witnessing his own existence as the very existence of the Truth, majestic is His majesty. Your living in ignorance is better than knowing these two groups, and your withdrawal from desires is better for you than being with them. And God is the One sought for help, and upon Him is reliance.

He forgives sin, relieves distress, removes hardship, mends the broken, enriches the poor, teaches the ignorant, guides the misguided, directs the bewildered, relieves the anguished, frees the captive, feeds the hungry, clothes the naked, heals the sick, grants well-being to the afflicted, accepts the penitent, rewards the good-doer, supports the wronged, breaks the tyrant, pardons the stumbling, covers the faults, grants security from terror, raises some peoples, and lowers others. He does not sleep, nor should He sleep. He lowers the scale of justice and raises it. The deeds of the night are raised to Him before the deeds of the day, and the deeds of the day before the deeds of the night.

His veil is light. Were He to unveil it, the glories of His Face would burn away everything within the reach of His sight from His creation.

His right hand is full and is not depleted by any expenditure, pouring forth continually by night and day.

Have you considered what He has spent since He created creation? Yet it has not diminished what is in His right hand.

The hearts of the servants and their foreheads are in His hand, and the reins of all affairs are bound to His decree and His measure.

(Section)

He said in *Tariq al-Hijratayn*:

He drives the decrees that He ordained fifty thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth to their appointed times, so that nothing among them precedes its time or delays from it. Rather, each of them He has enumerated, as His Book has enumerated it, His Pen has run with it, His judgment has taken effect in it, and His knowledge has preceded it. He alone disposes of all the kingdoms, with the disposal of a King who is Powerful, Dominant, Just and Merciful, whose sovereignty is complete, with no contender disputing His dominion and no opponent contesting it. His disposal within His kingdom revolves between justice, benevolence, wisdom, benefit and mercy, and His disposal does not depart from these.

In the *Tafsir* of the memorizer Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn Musa ibn Mardawayh, through the hadith of al-Hammani: Ishaq ibn Sulayman narrated to us from Mu'awiya ibn Yahya, from Yunus ibn Maysara, from Abu Idris, from Abu al-Darda, that he was asked about the words of the Most High: ﴿Every day He is engaged in a [new] matter﴾ [al-Rahman: 29]. He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about it, and he said: "Among His matters is that He forgives a sin, relieves a distress, raises a people and lowers others."

Also in it, through the hadith of Hammad ibn Salama: al-Zubayr Abu Abd al-Salam narrated to us from Ayyub ibn Abd Allah ibn Makriz, from his father, who said: Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: Indeed your Lord, Mighty and Majestic, has no night or day. The light of the heavens and the earth is from the light of His Face. Your days, in His sight, are twelve hours. Your deeds are presented to Him in the morning, three hours from the beginning of the day. He looks at what He dislikes in them, and becomes angry. The first to know of His anger are the bearers of the Throne. The bearers of the Throne, the curtains of the Throne, the angels brought near and all the other angels glorify Him. Gabriel blows into the horn, and no creature of Allah in the heavens or the earth fails to hear it except the two weights (the jinn and humankind). They glorify Him for three hours until the Most Merciful is filled with mercy. That makes six hours. Then He calls for the wombs and considers them for three hours: ﴿He shapes you in the wombs however He wills. There is no god but He, the Mighty, the Wise﴾ [Al 'Imran: 6], ﴿He grants to whom He wills females, and grants to whom He wills males﴾ [al-Shura: 49]. That makes nine hours. Then He calls for the provisions and considers them for three hours: ﴿He extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it﴾.

That makes twelve hours.

Then Abd Allah recited: ﴿Every day He is engaged in a [new] matter﴾, and then said: This is your matter and the matter of your Lord, Mighty and Majestic.

Al-Tabarani also mentioned it in *al-Mu'jam al-Kabir* by another route.

This is part of the completeness of His disposal over His kingdom, glorified is He. For if His disposal were confined to one aspect and one pattern, it would not be a complete disposal.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 55, verse 31:

His saying in this surah: ﴿Soon We will attend to you, O you two burdens﴾ is a warning to the two categories who are held accountable by the sacred law (al-shara'i').

Qatadah said: its meaning is the emptying of the world, its ending, the coming of the Hereafter, and the recompense therein, and Allah, glorified is He, is not occupied by one thing from another.

Al-faragh (emptiness, leisure, or completion) in the language has two aspects: emptiness from occupation, and faragh in the sense of intention (qasd).

In this place it is in the second sense, namely the intention to recompense them for their deeds on the Day of Recompense.

His saying: ﴿O assembly of jinn and humankind, if you are able to pass beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass through. You will not pass through except with authority﴾ [al-Rahman: 33]

In it there are two opinions. The first: if you are able to penetrate what is in the heavens and the earth in knowledge (ilman), that is, to know what is in them, then know it; but you will not know it except by authority (sultan), that is, except by a proof from Allah. According to this, penetration here means the penetration of the knowledge of the two burdens into the heavens and the earth.

The second: if you are able to escape from the subjugation of Allah and the place of His authority and dominion by passing through the regions of the heavens and the earth and leaving the place of Allah's rule and authority, then do so. It is known that this is impossible for you, for you are under My authority and in the place of My dominion and power wherever you are.

Al-Dahhak said: the meaning of the verse is, if you are able to flee at the time of death, then flee, for it will overtake you. These sayings take the address to them with this statement to be in this world.

There is another interpretation of the verse, which is that this address is in the Hereafter, when the angels surround the regions of the earth and the enclosure of the Fire encompasses the horizons, and the creatures flee and find no escape or outlet, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And O my people, I fear for you the Day of Calling Out, the Day you will turn back fleeing﴾ [Ghafir: 32-33]. Mujahid said: fleeing, not able to escape. Al-Dahhak said: when they hear the roaring of the Fire, they run away in flight, but they do not reach any region of the regions except that they find the angels in ranks, so they return to the place where they were. That is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the angel will be upon its borders﴾ [al-Haqqah: 17], and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O assembly of jinn and humankind, if you are able to pass beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass through.﴾

This opinion is more apparent, and Allah knows best.

So when the creatures appear and turn back fleeing, it will be said to them: ﴿If you are able to pass beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass through.﴾

That is, if you are able to surpass the regions of the heavens and the earth and thereby overcome your Lord so that He cannot punish you, then do so. It seems that what precedes and follows this verse supports this view: before it is ﴿Soon We will attend to you﴾ [al-Rahman: 31], which refers to the Hereafter, and after it is ﴿And when the sky is split open and becomes rose-colored like red leather﴾ [al-Rahman: 37], which also refers to the Hereafter.

Also, this is an address to all of humankind and the jinn, for it uses the general form, which is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O assembly of jinn and humankind﴾.

So all of them must share in hearing this address and its content. This occurs only when Allah gathers them in one plain, where the caller makes them hear and the sight reaches them.

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿If you are able﴾ and did not say "if you two are able," to address the group, as in another verse: ﴿O assembly of jinn and humankind, did there not come to you﴾ [al-An'am: 130].

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary on surah 55, verse 35:

And He, the Exalted, says: ﴿He will send upon you both﴾ [al-Rahman: 35], and He did not say "upon you" (plural), in order to indicate both categories: that is, it is not restricted to one category over the other, but rather it is sent upon both categories together.

Although this is intended by His words ﴿If you are able﴾ [al-Rahman: 33], addressing the group in the plural form is better, meaning: whoever among you is able.

The address in the dual in His words ﴿upon you both﴾ [al-Rahman: 35] is good for another reason.

It is in agreement with the endings of the verses (ru'us al-ayat), so the dual is joined to the dual. And in it there is equality between the two categories in the punishment, by explicitly naming them, so the wording does not allow the meaning to be either one of them alone. And Allah knows best.

Ibn Abbas said: "Al-shuwaz" is the flame without smoke, and "al-nuhas" is the smoke without flame.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 55, verse 39:

And the words of the Exalted: ﴿So on that Day, no one will be questioned about his sin, neither man nor jinn.﴾

So He attributed the sins to the two weighty ones (al-thaqalan, i.e., mankind and jinn), and this is evidence that they are equal in being held accountable (al-taklif).

Scholars differed regarding this negated questioning. It has been said: it refers to the time of resurrection and the moving toward the place of standing (al-mawqif). At that time they will not be asked, and they will be asked after the standing has been prolonged and they seek intercession with Allah that He judge them and relieve them from their present state.

It has also been said: what is negated is the questioning of inquiry and seeking information (su'al al-isti'lam wa al-istikhbar), not the questioning of reckoning and recompense (su'al al-muhasabah wa al-mujazah). That is, Allah already knows their sins, so He does not question them about them in the manner of one who wishes to know them, but rather He holds them to account for them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 55, verse 46–47:

﴿And for him who fears the standing before his Lord, there are two gardens.﴾

It has been said: he is the servant who desires disobedience, then recalls the standing of his Lord over him in this world and his standing before Him in the Hereafter, and so he leaves it for the sake of Allah.

(A subtle point)

Yahya ibn Ayyub said: In Madinah there was a young man whom ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) admired. One night, after the ʿIsha prayer, he went out, and a woman appeared before him and presented herself to him, and he was captivated by her, and she went off. He followed her until she stopped at her door, and he saw her, and his heart was stirred, and this verse came to his mind: ﴿Indeed, those who fear Allah, when an impulse from Satan touches them, remember [Allah], and at once they are seeing clearly.﴾

He fell unconscious. The woman looked at him, and he was like a corpse. She and a maidservant of hers kept helping each other with him until they laid him at the door of his house. His father came out and found him lying at the door of the house, afflicted. He carried him in and brought him in. He regained consciousness, and his father asked him, "What has befallen you, my son?" but he did not tell him. His father kept at him until he told him. When he recited the verse, he gave a gasp, and his soul departed. The news of his story reached ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him), and he said:

"Why did you not inform me of his death?" So he went until he stood at his grave and called out, "O so-and-so! ﴿And for him who fears the standing before his Lord, there are two gardens.﴾"

He heard a voice from within the grave: "My Lord has given me it, O ʿUmar."

Al-Hasan related this story from ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) in another form. He said: In the time of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) there was a young man who was constant in the mosque and in worship. A slave girl desired him, and he entertained the thought of her in his soul. Then he remembered and saw clearly, and he gave a gasp and fainted from it. His paternal uncle came and carried him to his house. When he regained consciousness he said, "O uncle, go to ʿUmar, convey my greetings to him, and say to him: what is the reward of one who fears the standing of his Lord?" The uncle informed ʿUmar, and he came to him, but he had died. Then ʿUmar said, "For you are two gardens."

In the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi, from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with them both), he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Dhu al-Kifl did not refrain from any sin he committed. A woman came to him, and he gave her sixty dinars on condition that he would lie with her. When he sat between her legs as a man sits with his wife, she trembled and wept. He said, 'Why are you weeping? Have I forced you?' She said, 'No, but this is an act I have never done, and only need drove me to it.' He said, 'Would you do this when you have never done it before?' Then he said, 'Go, and the dinars are yours.' Then he said, 'By Allah, Dhu al-Kifl will never disobey Allah again.' He died that same night, and in the morning it was written on his door: 'Allah has forgiven Dhu al-Kifl.'" Al-Tirmidhi said: This is a hasan hadith.

Abu Hurayrah and Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them) said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave a sermon before his death, and in his sermon he said: "Whoever has the power over a woman or a slave girl unlawfully, and leaves her out of fear of Allah, Allah will grant him security on the Day of the Great Terror, will forbid him the Fire, and will admit him to Paradise."

Malik ibn Dinar said: The Gardens of Bliss lie between Firdaws and the Gardens of ʿAdn. In them are maidens created from the rose of Paradise. They are inhabited by those who were inclined toward sins, but when they remembered Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, they became watchful of Him, and their necks bent from fear of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Maymun ibn Mihran said: Remembrance is of two kinds. Remembering Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, with the tongue is good, but better than it is that you remember Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, when you are about to commit His prohibitions.

Qatadah (may Allah be pleased with him) said: It has been related to us that the Prophet of Allah used to say: "No man is able to commit something forbidden and then leave it, out of nothing but fear of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, except that He will replace it for him in this world, before the Hereafter, with something better for him than that."

ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr said: The truthfulness of faith and its righteousness is that a man is alone with a beautiful woman and leaves her, leaving her only for the sake of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

(Section)

In the two Sahihs, from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ashʿari, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he said: "Two gardens of gold, their vessels and their adornments and what is in them; and two gardens of silver, their vessels and their adornments and what is in them; and nothing stands between the people and looking at their Lord except the cloak of greatness over His face, in the Garden of ʿAdn." And Allah, the Exalted, has said: ﴿And for him who fears the standing before his Lord, there are two gardens﴾, and He mentioned them, then said ﴿and besides them two gardens﴾.

So these are four, and there has been disagreement about His words ﴿and besides them﴾: does it mean that they are above them, or below them?

On two opinions:

One group said: "besides them" means nearer to the Throne than them, so they would be above them.

Another group said: "Rather, the meaning of 'besides them' is below them."

They said: This is what is transmitted in the language of the Arabs when they say: "This is besides this," meaning it is lower in rank, as one of them said to someone who had exaggerated his praise:

"I am below what you say, and above what you have in your own mind."

In al-Sihah (of al-Jawhari): "dun" is the opposite of "fawq" (above).

It indicates falling short of the goal. Then he said: "It is said: this is dun that," meaning it is nearer to it.

The context indicates the preference of the first two gardens over them in ten respects:

First: His words ﴿with branches﴾ (dhawata afnan). Regarding it there are two views: one is that it is the plural of fanan, which is a branch; the second is that it is the plural of fann, which is a kind, meaning possessing various kinds of fruits and other things. This is not mentioned concerning the two that follow them.

Second: His words ﴿in them are two flowing springs﴾.

Concerning the latter two: "in them are two gushing springs." The nadkhah is the one that gushes, and the jariyah is the one that flows freely; the latter is better than the gushing one, for it includes both gushing and flowing.

Third: He said ﴿in them of every fruit are two kinds﴾, while concerning the latter two: ﴿in them are fruit, and palm trees, and pomegranates﴾. There is no doubt that the description of the first two is more complete.

The two kinds have been disputed, after agreement that they are two types. 

One group said: the two kinds are fresh and dried, the dried one not falling short in its excellence and quality of the fresh, and one enjoys it as one enjoys the dried.

There is a view here that is not hidden.

Another group said: the two kinds are a known type and a type of a different form.

Another group said: two types, and they did not add more; and the apparent, and Allah knows best, is that it is the sweet, the sour, the white and the red, for the variety of kinds of fruit is more wondrous, more appetizing, and more delightful to the eye and the mouth.

Fourth: He said ﴿reclining on carpets whose linings are of brocade﴾.

This is an indication of the excellence and high value of the linings. Concerning the latter two He said ﴿reclining on green cushions and beautiful rugs﴾. The "rafraf" has been explained as cushions and spreads, and explained as carpets, and explained as cushions above them.

According to every view, He did not describe them with what He described the carpets of the first two gardens.

Fifth: He said ﴿and the fruit of the two gardens is near﴾, meaning close and easy, which they reach however they wish. This is not mentioned concerning the latter two.

Sixth: He said ﴿in them are those restraining their gaze﴾.

That is, they have restricted their gaze to their husbands, so they see no one else, out of their contentment with them and their love for them. This implies that their beauty does not allow their husbands to look at anyone else.

He said concerning the latter two ﴿maidens restrained in pavilions﴾. And one who restricts her gaze to her husband by her own choice is more perfect than one who is restricted by other than herself.

Seventh: He described them as resembling rubies and coral in the purity of their color, its radiance and beauty, and this is not mentioned in those that follow.

Eighth: He, glorified and exalted, said concerning the first two gardens: ﴿Is the reward of good other than good?﴾ This requires that their people be of complete, absolute goodness, so their reward is of complete goodness.

Ninth: He began with describing the first two gardens and made them a reward for one who fears His standing. This indicates that they are the highest reward of the one who fears His standing. He ordered the mentioned reward upon fear, as an effect follows its cause. Since those who fear are of two types, the near ones and the people of the right hand, He mentioned the two gardens of the near ones, then mentioned the two gardens of the people of the right hand.

Tenth: He said ﴿and besides them two gardens﴾, and the context indicates that it is the opposite of "above," as al-Jawhari said.

If it is said: How are these four gardens distributed over one who fears the standing of his Lord?

It is said: Since those who fear are of two types as we have mentioned, the near ones have the two high gardens, and the people of the right hand have the two gardens below them. If it is said: Are the two gardens for the whole group of those who fear, sharing them, or does each one have two gardens, which are two orchards?

It is said: There are two views among the exegetes on this.

The second view is preferred for two reasons: one from transmission, and the second from meaning. As for the transmitted one, those who hold this view have related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "They are two orchards in the meadows of Paradise."

As for the one from meaning, one of the two gardens is the reward for performing the commands, and the second is the reward for avoiding the prohibitions.

If it is said: How, in mentioning the women, did He say "in them" in both places, while when He mentioned the others He said "in them" (dual)?

It is said: When He mentioned the cushions, after them He said ﴿in them are good, beautiful women﴾.

Then He repeated it in the latter two gardens with this wording, so that the wording and the meaning correspond, and Allah knows best.

(Section: on whether the believers among the jinn are in Paradise)

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And for him who fears the standing before his Lord, there are two gardens﴾

And He mentioned what is in the two gardens, up to His words: ﴿Neither man nor jinn has touched them before them﴾.
