Reports have been transmitted concerning their thickness and height, if they are preserved; the meaning is the height of their place, as related by al-Tirmidhi from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His saying ﴿And upon raised couches﴾, that he said: "Their height is as the distance between the sky and the earth, and the journey between them is five hundred years."

Al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a gharib hadith; we do not know it except from the narration of Rushdin ibn Sa'd."

It has been said that the meaning is that the aforementioned height refers to the ranks and the couches being upon them.

I say: Rushdin ibn Sa'd has munkar narrations. Al-Daraqutni said: "He is not strong."

Ahmad said: "He does not care from whom he narrates, and there is no harm in him regarding softening-of-hearts narrations." He said: "I hope he is salih al-hadith."

Yahya ibn Ma'in said: "He is nothing."

Abu Zur'a said: "He is weak."

Al-Jawzajani said: "He has munkar narrations, and there is no doubt that he had poor memory, so nothing he alone narrates is relied upon."

Ibn Wahb narrated: "Amr ibn al-Harith narrated to us, from Darraj Abu al-Samh, from Abu al-Haytham, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said regarding His saying ﴿And upon raised couches﴾, he said:

"The distance between the two couches is as the distance between the sky and the earth."

This is more likely to be the preserved version, and Allah knows best.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 55, verse 56:

He, glorified be He, described them with restraint (qasr) in three places. The first is this one.

The second is His saying in al-Saffat: ﴿And with them are those restrained in glance, with beautiful eyes﴾.

The third is His saying in Sad: ﴿And with them are those restrained in glance, of equal age﴾.

All the exegetes agreed that the meaning is: they have restricted their gaze to their husbands, so they do not look longingly toward anyone else.

It was also said: their husbands restrict their gaze to them, so that their beauty and loveliness do not prevent them from looking at anyone other than them.

This is sound in meaning.

As for the wording: qasirat is a descriptive attribute (sifah) attached (idafah) to its agent, meaning "beautiful of faces."

Its original form is qasir tarfuhunna, that is, not one whose gaze roams and reaches out.

Adam said: Warqa' related to us from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿restrained in glance﴾:

He said: they restrain their gaze to their husbands, so they do not desire anyone other than their husbands.

Adam also said: al-Mubarak ibn Fadalah «1» related to us from al-Hasan, who said:

They restricted their gaze to their husbands, so they do not turn toward anyone else. By Allah, they are neither displaying their adornment nor casting longing glances.

Mansur related from Mujahid: they restricted their sight, their hearts, and their souls to their husbands, so they do not turn toward anyone else.

In the tafsir of Sa'id from Qatadah, he said: they restricted their glances to their husbands, so they do not turn toward anyone else.

As for "atrab (equal in age)": it is the plural of tirb, which is a person's peer (lidah).

Abu 'Ubaydah and Abu Ishaq said: "peers (aqran), whose ages are the same."

Ibn 'Abbas and the rest of the exegetes said: "equal in age, of one birth, daughters of thirty-three years."

Mujahid said: "atrab" means "similars (amthal)."

Abu Ishaq said: they are in the utmost youth and beauty, and a person's equal and companion is called tirbah, because he touches the dust of the earth together with him at the same time.

The meaning from the report that their ages are equal is that there are no elderly women among them whose beauty has passed, nor young girls who are not fit for intercourse, unlike the males, among whom are the wildan, who are the servants.

It has been disputed concerning the referent of the pronoun in His saying "in them" (fihinna).

One group said: its referent is the two gardens and what they contain of palaces, chambers and tents.

Another group said: its referent is the cushions mentioned in His saying: ﴿reclining on cushions whose linings are of brocade﴾, and "fi" here means "upon" (ala).

And His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Neither man nor jinn has touched them before them﴾

Abu 'Ubaydah said:

"Lam yamsahunna" (they have not touched them). It is said: "This camel has never been touched by a rope (ma tamatha hadha al-ba'ir hablun qatt)," meaning it has never been touched.

Yunus said: the Arabs say, "This is a camel that no rope has ever touched," meaning it has never been touched.

Al-Farra' said: al-tamth is deflowering (al-iftidad), which is intercourse accompanied by bleeding, and tamth is blood.

There are dialect forms: tamith (yatmath) and tamith (yatmith).

Al-Layth said: "tamathat al-jariyah" means when one deflowers the girl, and al-tamith in their language is the menstruating woman.

Abu al-Haytham said: it is said of a woman "tamathat (yatmath)" when she bleeds upon deflowering, and "tamitha 'alayya" (she did) yatmith, when she menstruates for the first time, so she is tamith.

He said, regarding the verse of al-Farazdaq:

"They came out to me, not deflowered before me, and they were purer than ostrich eggs"

meaning, they had not been touched.

The exegetes said: he did not have intercourse with them, did not cover them, and did not copulate with them. These are their words. They differ concerning these (women). Some say: they are those who were created in Paradise from its houris. Others say: it refers to the women of this world, who were re-created as a different creation, virgins, as they are described.

Al-Sha'bi said: they are women from among the women of this world, who have not been touched since they were created as a creation.

Muqatil said: because they were created in Paradise.

'Ata', from Ibn 'Abbas, said: they are the human women who died as virgins.

al-Kalbi said: no man or jinn has had intercourse with them in this creation in which they were created.

I say: the apparent meaning of the Qur'an is that these women are not from the women of this world, but are from the wide-eyed houris (al-hur al-'in).

As for the women of this world, the women of mankind have been touched by humans, and the women of the jinn have been touched by jinn. The verse indicates this.

Abu Ishaq said: in this verse there is evidence that the jinn can have intercourse just as humans can.

What indicates that they are the houris created in Paradise is that He, glorified be He, made them among what Allah has prepared in Paradise for its people, of fruits, produce, rivers, garments and other things.

The following verse also indicates it, which is His saying: ﴿Houris, restrained within the tents﴾, then He said: ﴿Neither man nor jinn has touched them before them﴾.

Imam Ahmad said: the wide-eyed houris do not die at the blowing of the Trumpet, because He created them for permanence.

In the verse there is evidence for the position taken by the majority: that believing jinn are in Paradise, just as their disbelievers are in the Fire.

al-Bukhari gave it a chapter heading in his Sahih, saying "Chapter: The reward and punishment of the jinn," and more than one of the salaf stated this explicitly.

Damrah ibn Habib, when asked whether the jinn have reward, said: yes, and recited this verse.

Then he said: human women are for humans, and jinn women are for jinn. Mujahid said regarding this verse: when a man has intercourse without mentioning the name of Allah, the jinn coils around his penis and has intercourse with it.

The pronoun in His saying "before them" (qablahum) refers to the two groups mentioned in "reclining" (muttakiin), and they are the husbands of these women.

(Benefit: on placing mankind before the jinn in some passages)

Al-Suhayli said:

As for His saying: ﴿Neither man nor jinn has touched them before them﴾,

and His saying: ﴿Of his sin, no man or jinn will be asked﴾,

and His saying: ﴿And we thought that man and jinn would never speak a lie against Allah﴾,

the word "jinn" here does not include the angels in any way, because they are free of defects, and it is not conceivable that they would lie or commit any of the other sins. Since the general wording of this context does not include them, it begins with "man," for their excellence and perfection.

Ibn al-Qayyim said:

As for placing man before the jinn in His saying: ﴿Neither man nor jinn has touched them before them﴾,

it is for another wisdom beyond what he mentioned. Negation follows what the hearts understand of affirmation, so the negation is directed at it. The souls' knowledge of men touching (women) and their aversion toward one whom men have touched is well known, so the negation came in accordance with that, and placing man first in this negation is more important. As for His saying: ﴿And we thought that man and jinn would never speak a lie against Allah﴾, its secret is known from the context, for this is a report of the speech of the believing jinn when they heard the Qur'an, as He, exalted be He, said: ﴿Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of the jinn listened, and they said: Indeed we have heard a wondrous Qur'an…﴾ and the verses that follow.

The Qur'an was first addressed to mankind and was revealed to their Prophet, and they were the first to affirm or deny it before the jinn. So the statement of the believing jinn, ﴿And we thought that man and jinn would never speak a lie against Allah﴾, placed man first because of their precedence in being addressed by the Qur'an and their precedence in affirmation and denial.

Another benefit: this is a report of the believing jinn's speech to their people after they returned to them and informed them of what they had heard of the Qur'an, its greatness, and its guidance to right conduct. Then they excused themselves for what they had previously believed, contrary to what they had heard of right guidance, by saying that they had not supposed that man and jinn would speak lies against Allah. Mentioning man first here is more effective in calling to the message and more conclusive in removing suspicion, for they opposed what they had heard from men and jinn once their lying became clear. Beginning with the mention of man is more emphatic in negating the purpose and the accusation, and so that their people would not suppose that they had aided men against them, for they were the first to acknowledge fabricating lies against Allah, the Exalted. This is among the most subtle and precise meanings, and whoever reflects on its placement in the discourse will know its soundness.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 55, verse 58:

And His saying: ﴿As if they were rubies and coral﴾

Al-Hasan and the majority of the exegetes said: It means the clarity of the ruby within the whiteness of the coral. They were likened, in clearness and whiteness of color, to the ruby and the coral. What supports this is what ʿAbdullah (Ibn Masʿud) said:

"Indeed, a woman among the women of the People of Paradise will be clothed in seventy garments of silk, and the whiteness of her shins will be seen through them from behind, because Allah says: ﴿As if they were rubies and coral﴾

Now, the ruby is a stone; if you were to put a thread in it and then polish it, you would see the thread from behind the stone."

Ibn Wahb said: Amr ibn al-Harith informed me, from Abu al-Samh, from Abu al-Haytham, from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿As if they were rubies and coral﴾

He said: "One looks at his own face in her cheek, clearer than a mirror. Indeed, the least pearl upon her would illuminate what is between the east and the west. And indeed, there will be upon her seventy garments, which his sight will penetrate until he sees the marrow of her shin through all of that."

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 55, verse 60:

It means: Is the recompense for one who worshipped his Lord well anything other than that his Lord should treat him well?

Ibn 'Abbas said: "Is the recompense of one who says 'There is no god but Allah' and acts according to what Muhammad brought anything other than Paradise?"

Ibn Abi Shaybah and others have mentioned, from the hadith of al-Zubayr ibn 'Adi, from Anas ibn Malik, who said:

"The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿Is the recompense for good anything but good?﴾

Then he said: Do you know what your Lord said?

They said: Allah and His Messenger know best.

He said: He says: Is the recompense of one upon whom I have bestowed Tawhid anything but Paradise?"

[Section: The Station of Ihsan]

Among the stations of ﴿You alone do we worship, and You alone do we ask for help﴾ is the station of Ihsan (excellence).

It is the core (lubb) of faith, its spirit and its perfection. This station encompasses all the stations, for all of them are folded within it. Everything that has been said from the beginning of the Book up to this point is part of Ihsan.

The author of "al-Manazil" (may Allah have mercy on him), citing this station, quoted the verse of the Most High:

﴿Is the recompense for good anything but good?﴾ [al-Rahman: 60].

So Ihsan comprises all the gates of the realities (haqa'iq). It is that you worship Allah as though you see Him.

As for the verse, Ibn 'Abbas and the exegetes said: Is the recompense of one who says "There is no god but Allah" and acts according to what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought anything but Paradise?

It has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he recited ﴿Is the recompense for good anything but good?﴾

Then he said: Do you know what your Lord said? They said: Allah and His Messenger know best. He said: He says: Is the recompense of one upon whom I have bestowed Tawhid anything but Paradise?

As for the hadith, it points to the perfection of presence with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and His all-encompassing vigilance (muraqabah), combining fear of Him, love and knowledge of Him, turning to Him in repentance, sincerity towards Him, and all the stations of faith.

[Degrees of Ihsan]

[The First Degree: Ihsan in Intention, by refining it with knowledge]

He said: It has three degrees. The first degree: Ihsan in intention, by refining it with knowledge, firming it with resolve, and purifying it in state.

That is: the excellence of intention is by three things.

The first: refining it with knowledge, by making it follow knowledge according to its requirement, refined by it, purged of the impurities of personal interests, so that one intends only what is permissible in knowledge. And knowledge is following the command and the Law.

The second: firming it with resolve. Ibram means firmness and strength.

That is, it is accompanied by a resolve that carries it through, not accompanied by lethargy and negligence that weakens and enfeebles it.

The third: purifying it in state.

That is, the state of its possessor should be clear of turbidities and impurities which indicate the murkiness of his intention.

For the state is the manifestation and fruit of intention, and it is also its material and its motivator. Each of them is affected by the other.

So its clarity and purification are part of the complete clarity and purification of the other.

[Section: The Second Degree: Ihsan in States]

He said: The second degree: Ihsan in states. It is that you guard them with jealousy, conceal them with refinement, and correct them through verification.

He means by guarding them: preserving and protecting them out of jealousy lest they depart, for they pass like clouds. If one does not observe their rights, they depart. Guarding them is through constancy in faithfulness and avoiding harshness.

One also guards them by honoring their guests, for they are a guest, and a guest who is not honored departs.

One also guards them by controlling them as a possession, holding one's hand firmly over them, and not letting them fall to a highway robber or plunderer.

One also guards them by submitting to their judgment and yielding to their authority when it agrees with the command.

One also guards them by concealing them with refinement, which is to hide them from people as far as possible, so that people do not know of them, and not to reveal them except for a proof, or a need, or a weightier benefit. For in revealing them without such reason there are many harms, along with exposing them to thieves, robbers, and raiders.

Revealing one's state to people, in the view of the truthful, is folly and weakness. It is among the portions of the self and of Satan. The people of truthfulness and resolve conceal them more than the owners of treasures conceal their wealth, to the point that some of them show their opposites by denial and repudiation. These are the people of the Malamatiyya (the blamers), who have a well-known path. The shaykh of this group was 'Abd Allah ibn Manazil.

The group agreed that whoever informs people of his state with Allah has defiled his path, except for a proof, a need, or a necessity.

As for his saying "and correct them through verification":

That is, he strives to verify his states, correct them and purify them.

For a state may be mixed with truth and falsehood, and only people of insight and knowledge can distinguish it.

The people of this path say: the incoming inspiration (warid) that the servant receives from his right side, and the voices and address, is in most cases true.

And that which comes from the left side is in most cases false and a lie.

For the people of the right are the people of truth; with their right hands they take their books, and their light shines on the Sirat before them on their right.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) liked to begin with the right in putting on his sandals, combing his hair, in his purification and in all his affairs.

Allah and His angels bless the right rows of the lines.

He informed that Satan eats with his left and drinks with his left, and his share of the son of Adam is the left side.

For this reason the left hand is used for istijmar (cleaning after relieving oneself) and removing filth and harm, and the left foot is begun with when entering the lavatory.

Among the criteria of discernment also: every inspiration after which a person remains energetic, joyful and elated is an angelic inspiration; and every inspiration after which a person remains with an evil soul, lazy, with heavy limbs and spirit, inclining towards lethargy, is a satanic inspiration.

Also among the criteria: every inspiration that leaves its possessor with advancement towards Allah the Most High and the Last Abode, and presence therein, so that he seems to see Paradise brought near and Hellfire kindled, is divine and angelic; its opposite is satanic and carnal.

Also among the criteria: every inspiration whose cause is sincere counsel in obeying the command, and sincerity and truthfulness therein, is divine and angelic. Otherwise it is satanic.

Also among the criteria: every inspiration by which the heart is illumined, the breast is expanded, and the heart is strengthened, is divine and angelic. Otherwise it is satanic.

Also among the criteria: every inspiration that gathers you to Allah is from Him; and every inspiration that scatters you from Him and takes you away from Him is from Satan.

Also among the criteria: the divine inspiration is only spent in nearness and obedience, and its cause is only nearness and obedience; its extractor is the command, and its director is the command. The satanic is the opposite.

Also among the criteria: the merciful inspiration does not contradict itself, nor vary, nor differ, but rather each part confirms the other; the satanic, by contrast, contradicts itself. And Allah, glorified is He, knows best.

[Section: The Third Degree: Ihsan in the Moment]

He said: The third degree: Ihsan in the moment (waqt). It is that you never depart from witnessing (mushahadah), never mix your aspiration with anyone, and make your migration to the Truth perpetual.

That is, you do not depart from the state of witnessing.

This is only attainable by the people of firm establishment (tamkin) who have triumphed over their souls and crossed the distances between the soul and the heart, and the distances between the heart and Allah, by striving against the brigands who stand on those distances.

His saying: "and never mix your aspiration with anyone."

That is: attach your aspiration to the Truth alone, and do not attach your aspiration to anyone other than Him, for that is shirk on the path of the truthful.

His saying: "and make your migration to the Truth perpetual."

That is: every one who turns to Allah with truthfulness and sincerity is among those who migrate to Him.

So he should not lag behind this migration; rather he should keep it perpetually until he reaches Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

"Nothing remains but a moment, then it passes, and the one who travels will be praised at the end of the journey."

For every heart there are two migrations to Allah, and they are an obligation binding upon it at every breath:

A migration to Allah, glorified is He, through Tawhid and sincerity, turning in repentance, love, fear, hope, and servitude.

And a migration to His Messenger (ﷺ): through making him the judge, submission, entrusting, yielding to his judgment, and receiving the rulings of the outward and inward from his niche (mishkat). So his worship through him is greater than the worship of a caravan through a skilled guide in the darkness of night and the bewilderments of the road.

Whoever does not have these two migrations in his heart, let him throw dust on his head.

Let him re-examine faith from its root, so that he may return behind himself to seek light, before being barred from it and told so on the Sirat, from behind the wall. And Allah is the One sought for help.

Ibn Abi Shaybah said: Yahya ibn Yaman narrated to us from Ash'ab, from Ja'far, from Sa'id, who said: "Nadlakhatan" (two gushing springs, ﴿فِيهِمَا عَيْنَانِ نَضَّاخَتَانِ﴾) means [gushing] with water and fruits.

And Ibn Yaman narrated to us from Abu Ishaq, from Aban, from Anas, who said: "Nadlakhatan" [means gushing] with musk and ambergris, which pour over the dwellings of the people of Paradise just as rain pours over the dwellings of the people of this world.

And Abdullah ibn Idris narrated to us from his father, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Bara', who said: "The two that flow" (﴿فِيهِمَا عَيْنَانِ تَجْرِيَانِ﴾) are better than the two gushing ones.

(Section)

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, both as a statement of his own (mawqūf) and as a statement traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) (marfūʿ):

"There is not a pomegranate among these pomegranates of yours except that it is pollinated with a seed from the pomegranates of Paradise."

The mawqūf version is more likely (ashbah).

Ḥarb and others related from ʿAli that he said: "Eat the pomegranate with its membrane (shaḥm), for it is the tanning (dibāgh) of the stomach."

The sweet pomegranate is hot and moist. It is good for the stomach and strengthens it by its gentle astringency (qabḍ laṭīf). It is beneficial for the throat, the chest and the lungs, and good for coughing. Its water loosens the bowels. It nourishes the body with a light, modest nourishment, and it is quickly dissolved because of its thinness and subtlety. It produces a slight heat and wind in the stomach, and for this reason it helps with sexual potency (al-bāh). It is not suitable for those with fever. It has a remarkable property: when eaten with bread, it prevents corruption (fasād) in the stomach.

Its sour variety is cold and dry, astringent and subtle. It benefits the inflamed stomach, promotes urine more than other kinds of pomegranate, calms yellow bile (ṣafrāʾ), stops diarrhea, prevents vomiting, and thins the excess humours (fuḍūl).

It extinguishes the heat of the liver and strengthens the organs. It is beneficial for yellow-bile palpitations (khafaqān ṣafrāwī), for the pains that afflict the heart and the mouth of the stomach, strengthens the stomach, repels its excess humours, and quells yellow bile (mirrah ṣafrāʾ) and blood.

If its juice is extracted with its membrane and cooked with a little honey until it becomes like an ointment, and it is applied to the eye as kohl, it cuts the yellowness from the eye and cleanses it of thick humours. If it is smeared on the gums, it benefits the ulcer (ʾakalah) that afflicts them. If their juice is extracted with their membranes, it loosens the bowels and expels putrid bitter humours, and it benefits long-lasting intermittent fevers (ḥummayāt al-ghibb al-mutaṭāwilah).

As for the bitter-sour pomegranate (al-rummān al-murr), it is intermediate in nature and action between the two types, and this one leans slightly toward the subtlety of the sour. The seed of the pomegranate with honey is a poultice (ṭilāʾ) for ringworm (dāḥis) and malignant sores. Its blossoms (aqmāʿuh) are for wounds. They said: whoever swallows three of the pomegranate's cups (junbudh) each year will be safe from ophthalmia (ramad) for the entire year.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 55, verse 70:

"Fa-l-khayrat" is the plural of khayrah, which is a lightened form of khayyirah, like sayyidah and layyinah. "Hisan" is the plural of hasanah.

Thus they are good in character, conduct and disposition, and beautiful in face. Waki' said: Sufyan narrated to us from Jabir, from al-Qasim, from Abu Barzah, from Abu 'Ubaydah, from Masruq, from Abdullah, who said:

"Every Muslim has a khayrah (a good wife), and every khayrah has a tent, and every tent has four doors. Through each door, every day, there comes to her a gift, a present and an honour that had not been hers before. No ill-tempered ones, no foul-smelling ones, no ones who spit, and no arrogant ones."

(Section)

In the Mu'jam of al-Tabarani: "Umm Salamah, may Allah be pleased with her, asked him and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, tell me about the words of the Most High: ﴿In them are good [and] beautiful ones﴾.'

He said: 'Good in character, beautiful in face.'"

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 55, verse 72:

"Al-maqsurat" means: those who are confined (al-mahbusat).

Abu 'Ubayda said: they remained secluded in tents (kharadna fi al-khiyam).

Likewise Muqatil said: [they are] in tents. There is also another meaning: that what is intended is that they are confined to their husbands, not seeing anyone else, while they are in tents. This is the meaning of the view of those who said: they are restricted to their husbands, so they do not look at anyone other than them, and do not aspire to anyone besides them. This was also mentioned by al-Farra'.

I say: this is the meaning of "qasirat al-tarf" (those who restrain their gaze), but those are restrained by themselves, whereas these are "maqsurat" (confined by others).

And his saying "fi al-khiyam" according to this view is an attribute of the hur (the bright-eyed maidens). That is, they are in the tents. It is not an object governed by "maqsurat." It seems that the proponents of this view interpreted it to mean that they are confined in the tents, not leaving them for the upper chambers and gardens.

The proponents of the first view respond to this: God, glory be to Him, described them with the attributes of veiled, protected women, and that is more eloquent in description. It does not follow from this that they do not leave the tents for upper chambers and gardens, just as the women of kings and those below them, who are veiled and protected, are prevented from going out on journeys and otherwise to a promenade, garden, or the like. Their necessary attribute is seclusion in the house, even though it may occur to them, together with servants, to go out to gardens and the like.

As for Mujahid, he said: "maqsurat" means their hearts are confined to their husbands, in tents of pearl.

The first attribute of these women has already been mentioned, that they are "restrainers of the gaze" (qasirat al-tarf), and these are described as "maqsurat."

Both attributes apply to both types, for they are attributes of perfection.

That attribute is the restraint of the gaze from aspiring to anyone other than husbands, and this attribute is their restraint from display (tabarruj), exposure, and appearing to men.

(Section: on the mention of their tents, their couches, their thrones, and their pavilions)

God Most High said: ﴿Bright-eyed maidens, confined in the tents﴾

In the two Sahihs, from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said:

"Indeed, for the believer in Paradise there is a tent of a single hollow pearl, sixty miles long, in which there are family members; the believer goes around among them, and they do not see one another."

In another wording of both: "In Paradise there is a tent of hollow pearl, sixty miles wide, in each corner of which are family members whom the others do not see; the believer goes around among them."

In another wording of both also: "The tent is a pearl whose length in the sky is sixty miles; in each corner of it are family members of the believer, whom the others do not see."

In al-Bukhari alone, in one wording: "its length is thirty miles." These tents are not the upper chambers and palaces, but rather tents in gardens and on riverbanks.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya said: al-Husayn ibn 'Abd al-Rahman related to us from Ahmad ibn Abi al-Hawari, who said: I heard Abu Sulayman say: the creation of the bright-eyed maidens (al-hur al-'in) is initiated; when their creation is complete, the angels pitch tents over them.

Some of them said: since they are virgins, and it is the custom of a virgin to be secluded in her canopy until her husband takes her, God Most High created the hur and secluded them in canopies of tents, so that He may bring them together with His friends in Paradise.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya said: Ishaq related to us, Waki' related to us, Sufyan related to us from Jabir from al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazza from Abu 'Ubayda from Masruq from 'Abd Allah, who said: For every Muslim there is a bright-eyed maiden (khayra), and for every khayra there is a tent, and for every tent there are four doors, through each of which there enters to her every day a gift, a present, and an honor that was not there before: not (women) who are "mizzat" nor "zafarat" nor "bakharat" nor "tammahat"; bright-eyed maidens, large-eyed, as if they were hidden eggs (bayd maknun).

'Ali ibn al-Ja'd related to us, Shu'ba related to us from 'Abd Allah ibn Maysara, who said: I heard Abu al-Ahwas narrate from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud concerning the words of God Most High: ﴿Bright-eyed maidens, confined in the tents﴾

He said: a hollow pearl.

'Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak related to us: Sulayman al-Taymi related to us from Qatada from Khulayd al-Qasri from Abu al-Darda', who said: The tent is a single pearl with seventy doors, all of them of pearl.

Ibn al-Mubarak said: Hammam related to us from Qatada from 'Ikrima from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, who said: The tent is a hollow pearl, a farsakh by a farsakh, having four thousand leaves of gold.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya said: Fudayl ibn 'Abd al-Wahhab related to us, Sharik related to us from Mansur from Mujahid: ﴿Bright-eyed maidens, confined in the tents﴾

He said: in tents of pearl, and the tent is one pearl.

Muhammad ibn Ja'far related to me: Mansur related to us: Yusuf ibn al-Sabbah related to us from Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, "Bright-eyed maidens, confined in the tents," he said: The tent is a pearl of hollow pearl, a farsakh in length and a farsakh in width, and it has a thousand doors of gold; around it is a pavilion whose circumference is fifty farsakhs; through each of its doors there enters upon them an angel with a gift from God, Mighty and Majestic, and that is His saying: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate﴾.

And God knows best.

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary on Surah 55, verse 76 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Therein are couches raised high, and cups set in place, and cushions arranged in rows, and carpets spread out.﴾

Hisham narrated from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "The rafraf (ar-rafraf) are the gardens of Paradise. The 'abqari (al-'abqari) are the finest carpets."

Isma'il ibn 'Ulayyah narrated from Abu Raja', from al-Hasan, concerning the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿reclining on green rafraf and beautiful 'abqari﴾. He said: "They are the spreads (al-busut)." He said: "The people of Madina also say: they are the spreads."

As for the namariq (cushions), al-Wahidi said: "They are the pillows, according to all scholars. Its singular is namaraqa, with a damma on the nun."

Al-Farra' related namaraqa with a kasra on the nun. Abu 'Ubayda recited:

"When the carpet of revelry is spread out and its rugs and cushions are brought near to its owner."

Al-Kalbi said: "Pillows arranged one beside another." Muqatil said: "They are pillows arranged upon the tanafis (rugs)."

Az-zarabi (the carpets) means spreads and tanafis (woven rugs). Their singular is zarbiyya, according to the consensus of the linguists and expositors. As for mabthuthah (spread out), it means laid out and scattered.

(Section)

As for the rafraf, al-Layth said: "It is a kind of green garment that is spread out. Its singular is rafrafa."

Abu 'Ubayda said: "The rawafif are spreads," and he recited Ibn Muqbil:

"We are those who alight, our sandals covered by fallen garments of silk and rafraf."

Abu Ishaq said: "They said: the rafraf here means the gardens of Paradise. They also said: the rafraf are cushions. They said: the rafraf are the coverings (al-mahabis). They said: the rafraf are the surplus of the coverings used as bedding."

Al-Mubarrad said: "It is the surplus of the garments which kings use for bedding and other things."

Al-Wahidi said: "It seems that this is the closest meaning, because the Arabs call the edge of a tent and the piece of cloth that hangs at the lower part of a tent a rafraf." From this is the hadith concerning the death of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The rafraf was raised, and we saw his face as if it were a leaf."

Ibn al-A'rabi said: "The rafraf here is the edge of the tent (al-fustat). The surplus of the coverings hanging below was likened to the edge of the tent, and so it was called rafraf."

I say: The root of this word is an edge or a side. From it comes the rafraf in a wall (a projecting ledge), and from it the rafraf, which is the edge of a tent and the sides of a coat of mail and what hangs from them; its singular is rafrafa. From it: "the bird fluttered (rafraf al-tayr) when it moved its wings around a thing, wishing to alight upon it." The rafraf are also green garments from which coverings are made; its singular is rafrafa. Anything that is left over from something and folded back is a rafraf. In the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud concerning the words of Allah the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿He certainly saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾, he said: "He saw a green rafraf that filled the horizon." It is in the two Sahihs.

(Section)

As for the 'abqari, Abu 'Ubayda said: "Everything made of spreads is 'abqari." He said: "They think it is a land where carpets are embroidered." Al-Layth said: "'Abqar is a place in the desert where there are many jinn; it is said: 'as if he were a jinn of 'Abqar.'"

Abu 'Ubayda said, concerning the hadith of the Prophet (ﷺ) when he mentioned 'Umar: "I have not seen an 'abqari who drives his herd like him." The origin of this, it is said, is that it was attributed to 'Abqar, a land inhabited by jinn, and so it became a proverb for everything attributed to something lofty. He recited Zuhayr:

"Over them is a garden of jinn-like 'abqari; they are worthy one day of attaining and of being employed."

Abu al-Hasan al-Wahidi said: "This view is the correct one regarding the 'abqari. The Arabs, when they exaggerate in describing a thing, attribute it to the jinn or liken it to them." From this is the saying of Labid:

"The jinn of destruction have made firm their feet."

Another said describing a woman:

"A jinniyya, and she has a jinn teaching her, who shoots hearts with a bow that has no string."

This is because they believe that the jinn possess every wondrous quality, and that they produce every marvelous thing. Since 'Abqar was known as their dwelling place, they attributed to it everything in which they exaggerated, meaning by that that it is from their work and craft. This is the origin; then 'abqari became an adjective for anything whose description is exaggerated.

Zuhayr's verse supports what we have mentioned, for he attributed the jinn to 'Abqar. Then we have seen many things attributed to 'Abqar other than spreads and garments, such as his description of 'Umar as "'abqari." Salama narrated from al-Farra' who said: "The 'abqari is the rightly-guided man, and the excellent of animals and jewels." If 'Abqar were specific to embroidery, then nothing other than the embroidered would be attributed to it; but what is attributed to it is the wondrously crafted embroidered spreads, as we have mentioned, just as everything exaggerated in description is attributed to it.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "'Abqari means spreads and tanafis." Al-Kalbi said: "They are the beautified tanafis." Qatada said: "They are the finest zarabi." Mujahid said: "They are thick brocade."

'Abqari is a plural whose singular is 'abqariyya, and it takes the description of a plural. So consider how Allah the Glorified and Exalted described the furnishings as raised high, the carpets as spread out, and the cushions as arranged in rows. The raising of the furnishings indicates their thickness and softness; the spreading of the carpets indicates their abundance and that they are everywhere, not reserved for the head of the gathering rather than its rear; and the description of the cushions indicates that they are prepared for leaning upon always, not stored away to be brought out at one time and not another.

(Section)

Paradise has several names according to its attributes, while its named reality is one according to its essence. Thus they are synonymous from this aspect, and they differ according to their attributes, so they are distinct from this aspect. Likewise are the names of the Lord, the Glorified and Exalted, the names of His Book, the names of His Messengers, the names of the Last Day, and the names of the Fire.

The first name: "al-Jannah" (the Garden). It is the general name that encompasses that abode and what it contains of kinds of bliss, pleasure, delight, joy, and the coolness of the eyes.

The origin of the derivation of this word is from concealment and covering. From it comes janin (the fetus), because it is hidden in the belly; and jann (the jinn), because it is hidden from the eyes; and mijann (the shield), because it covers and protects the face; and majnun (the insane), because his intellect is concealed and hidden from him. Also janna, which is the small thin snake. From it is the saying of the poet:

"She was fine-boned, shapely, slender and full, so if a human were concealed by her beauty, he would be concealed."

That is, if she were covered and hidden from the eyes, she would do that. From it the orchard is called jannah, because it conceals what is within it with trees and covers it. This name deserves to be applied only to a place with many trees of various kinds.

The janna, with a damma, is that with which one is shielded, such as a shield or other thing. From it is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They have taken their oaths as a shield, and thus they hide behind them from the denial of the believers.﴾ From it also is the janna, with a kasra, which means the jinn, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿from among the jinn and mankind.﴾

Some of the exegetes held that the angels are called janna. They argued with the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And they have made between Him and the janna a kinship.﴾ They said: "This kinship is their saying: the angels are the daughters of Allah." They preferred this view on two grounds.

The first: the kinship they claimed was only believed to exist between Him and the angels, not between Him and the jinn.

The second: the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And the janna certainly know that they will be brought forward (for punishment).﴾ That is, the angels certainly know that those who uttered this claim will be brought forward for punishment.

The correct view is contrary to what these held, and that the janna are the jinn themselves, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿from among the jinn and mankind.﴾

On this basis there are two opinions regarding the verse.

The first is the view of Mujahid, who said: "The disbelievers of Quraysh said: the angels are the daughters of Allah." Abu Bakr said to them: "Then who are their mothers?" They said: "The chieftains of the jinn."

Al-Kalbi said: "They said: He married among the jinn, and from their union the angels issued."

Qatada said: "They said: He became related by marriage to the jinn."

The second opinion is the view of al-Hasan. He said: "They associated the devils with the worship of Allah. This is the kinship they made."

The correct view is that of Mujahid and others.

What the proponents of the first view argued is not necessarily valid for their claim. For when they said, "The angels are the daughters of Allah, and they are of the jinn," they established a kinship between Him and the janna through this begetting, and made this kinship arise between Him and the jinn.

As for His saying: ﴿And the janna certainly know that they will be brought forward﴾, the pronoun refers to the janna. That is, the janna certainly know that they will be brought forward for the reckoning. This is what Mujahid said. That is, if there were a kinship between Him and them, they would not be brought to the reckoning, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the Jews and the Christians said: We are the sons of Allah and His beloved. Say: Why then does He punish you for your sins? Rather, you are human beings from among those He created.﴾ So He, the Glorified, made their punishment for their sins and their being brought forward for punishment a refutation of their false claim.

This interpretation of the verse is more emphatic in refuting their saying than the first interpretation, so consider it.

The second name: Dar as-Salam (the Abode of Peace). Allah named it by this name in His saying: ﴿For them is the Abode of Peace with their Lord﴾, and His saying: ﴿And Allah calls to the Abode of Peace.﴾

It is more deserving of this name, for it is the abode of safety from every calamity, blight, and displeasure. It is the abode of Allah. And His name, the Glorified and Exalted, is "as-Salam" (the Peace), who has made it safe and made its people safe. Their greeting therein is "Peace." ﴿And the angels enter upon them from every gate: Peace upon you, for what you endured with patience.﴾ The Lord, the Exalted, greets them from above them, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿For them therein is fruit, and for them is whatever they ask. Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful.﴾

And there is the hadith of Jabir concerning the greeting of the Lord, the Exalted, upon the people of Paradise. All their speech therein is peace; that is, there is no idle talk in it, nor indecency, nor falsehood, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They will not hear therein any idle talk, only "Peace, peace."﴾

As for His saying the Exalted: ﴿And as for one who is of the companions of the right, "Peace be upon you, from the companions of the right."﴾, most of the exegetes have circled around its meaning without reaching the core of what it intends, and they have stated views whose remoteness from the intended meaning is not hidden.

The meaning of the verse, and Allah knows best, is: "Peace be upon you, O you who departs from the world while you are of the companions of the right." That is, "Peace be upon you, being of the companions of the right, who were safe from the world and its miseries, and from the Fire and its punishment." So he is given good news of safety at his departure from the world and his arrival before Allah, just as the angel gives good news to his soul when he takes it, saying: "Rejoice in rest and provision, and a Lord who is not angry."

This is the first of the good tidings that the believer receives in the Hereafter.

The third name: Dar al-Khuld (the Abode of Eternity). It was so named because its people never depart from it forever, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿a gift that is never cut off﴾, and He said: ﴿Indeed this is Our provision, which has no end.﴾ And He said: ﴿Its food is constant, and its shade.﴾ And He said: ﴿and they will never be removed from it.﴾

The fourth name: Dar al-Muqama (the Abode of Lasting Residence). Allah the Exalted related the words of its people: ﴿And they say: "Praise be to Allah, who has removed grief from us. Indeed, our Lord is Most Forgiving, Most Appreciative, who has made us reside in the abode of lasting residence by His bounty; no fatigue touches us therein."﴾

Muqatil said: "He caused us to dwell in the abode of eternity; they remain in it forever, neither dying nor moving from it ever."

Al-Farra' and az-Zajjaj said: "Al-muqama is like al-iqama (residence). It is said: I resided in the place, a residence, a muqama, and a muqam."

The fifth name: Jannat al-Ma'wa (the Garden of Refuge). Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Near it is the Garden of Refuge.﴾

The sixth name: Jannat 'Adn (the Gardens of Eden). It was said: it is the name of one particular garden among the gardens. The correct view is that it is the name of the totality of the gardens, all of which are Gardens of Eden. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Gardens of Eden, which the Most Merciful has promised to His servants in the unseen.﴾

And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Gardens of Eden, they will enter them, adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their clothing therein is silk.﴾

And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and good dwellings in Gardens of Eden.﴾

The derivation indicates that all of them are Gardens of Eden, for it derives from residence and permanence. It is said: "'Adana bil-makan" (he resided in the place) when he remained there. "'Adantu al-balad" means I settled the town. "'Adanat al-ibil bi-makan kadha" means the camels remained in such a place and did not depart from it.

Al-Jawhari said: "From it [comes] Gardens of 'Adn," that is, residence.

From it is named al-ma'dan (the mine), with a kasra on the dal, because people reside in it in summer and winter. The center of everything is its ma'dan. And al-'adin is the she-camel that remains in the pasture.

The seventh name: Dar al-Hayawan (the Abode of Life). Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed the Abode of the Hereafter, that is the Life.﴾

What is meant, according to the exegetes, is the Garden. They said: "The Hereafter, meaning the Garden, is indeed the Life; it is the abode of life in which there is no death."

Al-Kalbi said: "It is a life in which there is no death."

Az-Zajjaj said: "It is the abode of enduring life." The linguists held that hayawan has the meaning of hayah (life). Abu 'Ubayda and Ibn Qutayba said: "Hayah and hayawan are the same." Abu 'Ubayda said: "Hayah, hayawan, and hayy (with a kasra on the ha') [are all forms of the same]." Abu 'Ali said: "He means that they are verbal nouns."

So hayah is of the pattern fa'la, like jalba (a commotion); hayawan is of the pattern fa'lan, like nazwan and ghalayan (boiling); and hayy is of the pattern fa'il, like 'ayy (incapacity). Al-'Ajjaj said:

"We were there when life was alive."

That is, when life was life. As for Abu Zayd, he differed from them and said: "Hayawan is that which has a soul, and mawtan (dead) is that which has no soul."

The correct view is that hayawan applies in two ways.

The first is as Abu 'Ubayda related.

The second is as an adjective, as Abu Zayd related.

According to Abu Zayd's view, hayawan is like hayy (living), the opposite of mayyit (dead).

The first view was preferred on the ground that the pattern fa'lan generally forms verbal nouns, like nazwan and ghalayan, unlike adjectives, whose pattern is fa'lan, like sakran and ghadaban.

Those who preferred the second view replied that fa'lan has also come in adjectives. They said: "Rajul dami'an (a man who is quick and light)" and "zafyan (quick)." In the Sihah: "A zafyan she-camel is swift; a zafyan bow is quick in releasing the arrow."

So Allah's saying: ﴿And indeed the Abode of the Hereafter, that is the Life﴾ allows two meanings.

The first: that the life of the Hereafter is life itself, because there is no disturbance in it, and no end to it; that is, nothing afflicts it that afflicts life in this abode. So hayawan here is a verbal noun.

The second: that the meaning is that it is the abode that does not perish, does not cease, and does not come to nothing, as the living perish in this world. Thus it is more deserving of this name than the hayawan that perishes and dies.

The eighth name: al-Firdaws (the Paradise). Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Those are the inheritors who will inherit the Firdaws; therein they will abide forever.﴾

And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, those who believed and did righteous deeds, for them are the Gardens of Firdaws as a lodging, abiding therein forever, desiring no change from it.﴾

The ninth name: Jannat an-Na'im (the Gardens of Bliss). Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, those who believed and did righteous deeds, for them are the Gardens of Bliss.﴾

This is also a comprehensive name for all the gardens, because of what it includes of the kinds by which its people enjoy bliss: food, drink, clothing, beautiful forms, a pleasant fragrance, a delightful sight, spacious dwellings, and other outward and inward bliss.

The tenth name: al-Maqam al-Amin (the Secure Station). Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in a secure station.﴾

The eleventh and twelfth names: Maq'ad as-Sidq (the Seat of Truth) and Qadam as-Sidq (the Station of Truth).

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be among gardens and rivers, in a seat of truth.﴾

He named His garden "a seat of truth" because every desired thing of a good seat is attained therein, just as it is said: "a sincere affection (mawaddah sadiqah)" when it is firm and complete, "a sincere sweetness (halawa sadiqa)," and "a sincere attack (hamla sadiqa)." From this comes "a truthful statement (al-kalam al-sidq)," because its intended purpose is attained by it.

The place of this word in their speech is soundness and perfection.

From it: truthfulness in speech, and truthfulness in action. The siddiq is the one whose word is confirmed by action.

As-sidq, with a fatha on the sad and the dal, means the firm part of spears. It is said of a brave man: "He is one of truthful attack (dhu sidq)," that is, his attack is genuine. "This is the confirmation (musaddiq) of this," that is, what confirms it. From it comes as-sadaqa (friendship), for the purity of affection and companionship. From it: "the fighting proved true to me (sadaqani al-qital)" and "affection proved true to me (sadaqani al-mawaddah)." From it: "a truthful advance (qadam sidq)," "a truthful tongue (lisan sidq)," "a truthful entrance (madkhal sidq)," and "a truthful exit (makhraj sidq)." All of this is for the established, intended truth that is desired, unlike the false lie, which has nothing beneath it, and which never contains a firm matter at all.

Some folk explained "qadam sidq" as the Garden. Others explained it as the deeds by which the Garden is attained. Others explained it as the precedence that Allah had decreed for them. Others explained it as the Messenger by whose hand and guidance they attained it.

The verified view is that all of these are true. For they have had the best (al-husna) decreed for them by Allah through that precedence, that is, through the causes He put forward for them by the hand of His messengers, and He stored up their reward for the Day of Resurrection. As for "lisan sidq," it is the tongue of true praise for the good deeds and the beautiful ways.

In its being "a tongue of truth": this indicates that it conforms to reality, and that it is praise rightfully due and not based on falsehood. The "entrance of truth" and the "exit of truth" are the entrance and exit in which the one who enters and exits is guaranteed by God. This means entering and exiting by God and for God. This supplication is among the most beneficial supplications for a servant, for he is always entering into some matter. Whenever his entering is for God and by God, and his exiting is likewise, he has entered an entrance of truth and exited an exit of truth. And God is the One sought for help.
